stages.message_model: Distilling raw source material into audience, core thesis, supporting claims and available evidence.
stages.outline: Ordering claims into a narrative sequence of slides and sections.
stages.slide_spec: Writing each slide's claim, choosing its layout and placing its primary evidence.
stages.editorial: Deciding which evidence stays on the slide and which moves to speaker notes or the appendix, and recording why.
stages.renderer: Laying out slides and drawing charts in the template.
stages.notes: Writing speaker notes and appendix or expandable-layer content.
stages.qa: Reviewing a finished draft for problems before a human sees it.

changes.reason: Absorbs DSN-28 and NAR-12. Resolves the DSN headline-length tension: the 'six words per headline' figure contradicted this rule, which has support from 13 books across 11 authors, so it was dropped.
Absorbs DSN-01, which stated the same rule plus the two-sub-point limit and squint test.
Absorbs CLM-21 (fragments live, sentences read). Adds the headline exemption so this rule no longer reads as contradicting CLM-01.
Absorbs FAIL-12 ('never put complete sentences on a slide'), rescoped to live body text so it no longer contradicts assertion headlines or slidedoc rules.
Rescoped to live body text. Unscoped, it contradicted SPW-04, SPW-19, and DSN-56.
Absorbs FAIL-26 (show full content at once). DSN-08 already resolves the split: progressive reveal for complex diagrams and charts, never line-by-line reveal of text lists.
Harmonized from 'four to six' to three to five so it agrees with NAR-08 (strong, more authors) and CLM-33 on nesting.
The original allowed three to four levels of bullet nesting inside a slide, which contradicted CLM-33 and DSN-05.
Resolves the DSN on-slide text tension: 30 words is the live body target and 75 words the hard ceiling. The 'six words per slide' figure is dropped because it conflicts with assertion headlines.
Absorbs EVD-72 (hook accuracy). Removes humor from acceptable opening hooks to resolve the NAR humor-timing tension.

Absorbs NAR-48 and FAIL-28 into one humor rule. Resolves the humor-timing tension in favor of alley-craft and abela-advanced (two authors) over reynolds-zen (one), since credibility risk is highest in the opening. Brand profiles may override this rule.

rules.rule: Define the presentation's purpose as the specific decision, action, or belief-change the audience should take away, not as information the presenter wants to deliver.
rules.applies_when: always, at the start of message modeling
rules.check: The stated objective names an audience decision, action, or belief-change, not a presenter activity like 'inform' or 'update'.
rules.prevents: unfocused decks that inform without moving the audience toward a decision

rules.rule: Before drafting, document who the primary audience is, their current position on the topic (unaware, skeptical, evaluating, or already committed), their decision authority, and their likely objections or constraints.
rules.applies_when: always, before content is drafted
rules.check: A documented audience profile exists covering identity, current position, decision authority, and known objections, and slide_spec decisions reference it.
rules.prevents: building a deck that answers the wrong question or ignores the audience's real constraints

rules.rule: When distinct audience segments (e.g., lead investor vs. syndicate, board vs. LPs) have materially different expertise, needs, or decision authority, build separate tracks of content for each rather than one generic version for everyone.
rules.applies_when: audience contains segments with materially different needs or authority
rules.check: Segments with divergent needs have either separate decks/appendices or clearly labeled sections addressing each.
rules.prevents: a deck that satisfies no one because it is diluted across incompatible audience needs

rules.rule: When the audience mixes domain experts with non-expert decision-makers, keep each slide's stated claim in plain language and move technical methodology, jargon-heavy evidence, and detailed justification to speaker notes or the appendix.
rules.applies_when: audience includes both specialist and non-specialist members
rules.check: Main slide claims are readable without domain training; technical justification needed only by specialists is in notes/appendix.
rules.prevents: alienating non-experts with jargon, or boring and under-serving experts by omitting rigor entirely
rules.note: Absorbs AUD-04. If a technical term is spoken aloud, show it as an on-screen label too (SPW-02).

merged_from.rule: Strip dense, jargon-heavy, or long/complex sentences from the slide face; if precise technical wording is necessary, move it to speaker notes or the appendix. Keep the on-slide visual simple even when the underlying idea is complex, without oversimplifying to the point of misrepresenting it.
merged_from.check: Read the slide text aloud — does any sentence require rereading, or use undefined terms? Does the slide read clearly at a glance while notes/appendix carry the necessary nuance?

rules.rule: For audiences that are already expert in the foundational material, cut basic background and definitions entirely and lead with novel findings, principles, and strategic implications instead.
rules.applies_when: audience is composed of domain experts already familiar with standard background
rules.check: No slide explains foundational concepts the stated expert audience already knows; early slides state novel findings, not setup.
rules.prevents: wasting expert attention and credibility on redundant scaffolding (the expertise-reversal effect)
rules.note: Distinguished from the mixed-audience layering rule: this applies only when the whole audience is expert, whereas layering applies when experts and non-experts are both present and basics still serve the non-experts.

rules.rule: For audiences with low expertise in the subject, pair explanatory text with a visual and explicitly connect new technical claims to a concept the audience already knows; for expert audiences, either text or visual alone is sufficient and the extra scaffolding can be cut.
rules.applies_when: audience expertise in the specific technical domain is known or can be estimated
rules.check: Technical claims aimed at non-experts include both an explanatory visual and an explicit link to a familiar concept; the same claims for expert audiences don't carry redundant scaffolding.
rules.prevents: novices unable to integrate new information; experts bored by unnecessary explanation

rules.rule: Match vocabulary to audience expertise — define or avoid jargon for non-specialists, use precise consistent technical terms for specialists — and never switch between two names for the same concept.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: Every technical term is either appropriate to the stated audience's expertise or defined on first use; the same concept is named identically throughout.
rules.prevents: jargon barriers for general audiences and inconsistent-naming confusion for anyone

merged_from.rule: Use plain, jargon-free language and define any unavoidable technical term on first use for audiences that lack domain expertise (generalist investors, LPs, boards); reserve unexplained domain terminology and acronyms for audiences who share the relevant technical background (internal teams, subject-matter reviewers).
merged_from.check: Identify the intended audience; if non-expert, confirm every specialized term or acronym is either avoided or defined at first use.

merged_from.rule: Calibrate how much evidence is explained, how much jargon is left undefined, and how much supporting detail is shown to the audience's actual expertise: define specialized terms at first use and simplify or remove evidence pitched above a non-specialist audience's level, while expert audiences can be given denser, less-explained evidence.
merged_from.check: general/mixed-expertise versions of a slide define jargon at first appearance and drop evidence a non-specialist couldn't interpret unaided; expert-audience versions can skip those definitions and carry denser evidence

rules.rule: Frame the audience, not the presenter or company, as the central actor: state problems as things the audience experiences or stands to lose, and state solutions as things the audience can do or gain.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: Problem and benefit statements are phrased in terms of audience consequences and audience actions, not presenter accomplishments or presenter needs.
rules.prevents: audiences disengaging from content that reads as self-serving or irrelevant to them

merged_from.rule: Frame the narrative and its evidence around the audience's own decision or situation, not as a showcase of the presenter's or company's expertise.
merged_from.check: For each major claim, is the framing 'here's what this means for your decision/return/risk' rather than 'here's how sophisticated our work is'?

rules.rule: Identify audience-specific objections, constraints (budget, authority, timeline, prior commitments), and any stakeholders outside the room who could block the decision, and address them directly rather than presenting an idealized version of the ask.
rules.applies_when: the deck requests a decision or action with known practical constraints or blockers
rules.check: Known constraints and likely objections are explicitly named and addressed somewhere in the deck or notes, not assumed away.
rules.prevents: a recommendation dismissed as impractical, or derailed later by an unaddressed stakeholder

rules.rule: When the audience's preferred way of absorbing information is known (e.g., numbers over narrative, terse over exhaustive, a specific executive's known style), adapt the deck's format and detail level to match it rather than defaulting to the presenter's own preference.
rules.applies_when: audience's format or detail preference is known or documented
rules.check: Format and depth choices reference a documented audience preference, not just the default template.
rules.prevents: a technically sound deck that fails because it is delivered in a format the audience doesn't absorb well

rules.rule: Default to framing risk and competitive threats in terms of what the audience stands to lose by not acting, rather than only what they stand to gain, since loss framing is generally more motivating.
rules.applies_when: choosing how to frame a risk, threat, or opportunity
rules.check: Risk/opportunity slides state the cost of inaction, not only the upside of acting.
rules.prevents: underselling the urgency of a risk by framing it only as forgone upside

rules.rule: Evaluate and present a recommendation against the audience's own stated decision criteria and known constraints, not an idealized or generic benchmark.
rules.applies_when: presenting a recommendation for approval
rules.check: Evaluation metrics and comparisons cited on the slide match criteria the specific audience is known to use.
rules.prevents: a recommendation that looks strong by generic standards but fails the audience's actual test

rules.rule: When asking an executive or board to approve something, frame the ask's success in terms of the performance metric(s) that stakeholder already uses to judge outcomes, not as a binary completed activity.
rules.applies_when: audience is an executive or board member who tracks specific KPIs
rules.check: The recommendation's stated benefit is expressed as a measurable metric the audience already tracks, not just 'done/not done'.
rules.prevents: a recommendation that reads as an activity report rather than a lever on something the executive cares about

rules.rule: When the audience doesn't already trust the presenter, establish credibility early with specific relevant accomplishments (not irrelevant biography), name and defer to any recognized domain expert in the audience, and frame the presenter's role as serving the audience's outcome rather than proving their own authority.
rules.applies_when: audience does not already know or trust the presenter, or includes a named domain expert
rules.check: Opening material states specific relevant accomplishments; a named expert in the audience is acknowledged if present; framing emphasizes audience benefit over presenter authority.
rules.prevents: audience skepticism toward claims, or an expert audience member feeling dismissed

rules.rule: Choose narrative order based on audience trust and disposition: for audiences that already trust the presenter or are outcome-focused, lead with the recommendation and follow with support; for unfamiliar, skeptical, or antagonistic audiences, build up through the shared question and problem first, delay stating the conclusion, and acknowledge the strongest opposing arguments before presenting the recommendation.
rules.applies_when: condition on the audience's documented trust/disposition toward the presenter and the claim
rules.check: Trusting/favorable-audience decks lead with the ask; unfamiliar/skeptical-audience decks open with the shared question and address counterarguments before the recommendation.
rules.prevents: an unfamiliar or skeptical audience dismissing a conclusion before hearing the reasoning, or a trusting audience losing patience with unnecessary build-up
rules.note: Alley's antagonistic-audience rule and Knaflic's trust-based ordering rule describe the same underlying variable (audience disposition); merged into one conditional rule rather than treated as separate or conflicting guidance.

rules.rule: Calibrate how much speculative or uncertain material to expose based on audience risk tolerance: minimize or clearly flag speculation for high-stakes decision-makers like funders and boards, and reserve fuller exploratory discussion for expert peer audiences.
rules.applies_when: content includes speculative, preliminary, or uncertain claims
rules.check: Speculative claims presented to funders/boards are flagged as such or omitted; fuller speculative discussion appears only in peer-audience or appendix material.
rules.prevents: presenting speculative ideas as established fact to decision-makers

rules.rule: When the audience may include non-native speakers of the presentation language or the content uses unfamiliar terminology, back any narration or spoken explanation with on-screen text or captions, and avoid idioms, false cognates, and culture-specific references.
rules.applies_when: audience may include non-native speakers or the content is unfamiliar/specialized
rules.check: Key narrated points have corresponding on-screen text; idioms and culture-specific references are absent.
rules.prevents: comprehension loss from relying on transient speech or culture-bound language

rules.rule: Match the formality of tone in narration and speaker notes to the audience's cultural and professional communication norms rather than defaulting to a casual house style.
rules.applies_when: audience has a known cultural or professional preference for formal communication
rules.check: Narration/notes tone is checked against the stated audience's formality expectations before finalizing.
rules.prevents: discomfort or distraction from tone perceived as inappropriately casual

rules.rule: Do not vary slide design, sequencing, or content modality based on claimed individual learning-style or personality categories (e.g., 'visual learner'); base adaptation only on measurable factors such as domain expertise, stakes, and decision role.
rules.applies_when: considering whether to customize design for individual audience members
rules.check: Design rationale cites expertise, stakes, or role — not a learning-style or personality-type label — as the reason for any audience-specific variation.
rules.prevents: wasted effort customizing for a categorization with no empirical support
rules.note: Several single-source practitioner rules proposing to design around audience personality-type dimensions (e.g., MBTI) were dropped as uncheckable and, per the precedence given to empirical findings on comprehension, superseded by this research-based rule.

rules.rule: Scale decorative color use inversely to audience motivation and stakes: restrict color to functional highlighting for expert, high-stakes, or time-pressed decision-makers (e.g., investors, boards), and reserve broader decorative color for lower-stakes, less-motivated general audiences.
rules.applies_when: choosing how much decorative color to use
rules.check: High-stakes expert-audience decks use color only to highlight key data/claims; decorative color is minimal.
rules.prevents: wasting the cognitive effort of a motivated audience on decorative processing, or under-using color's persuasive value for a disengaged audience

rules.rule: Ground claims and evidence in what the audience already knows, values, or cares about, rather than assuming they share the presenter's priorities or introducing values they don't yet hold.
rules.applies_when: selecting and framing evidence
rules.check: Each major claim connects explicitly to something the stated audience already values or understands, not solely to the presenter's priorities.
rules.prevents: a technically sound argument that the audience perceives as disconnected from their reality

rules.rule: Identify which phase of the decision or adoption process the audience currently occupies (e.g., first meeting vs. diligence vs. final close) and design the ask to move them to the next phase, not to a final commitment prematurely.
rules.applies_when: the relationship with the audience spans multiple stages before a final decision
rules.check: The stated call to action matches the audience's current phase rather than jumping to a final commitment.
rules.prevents: asking for more commitment than the relationship stage supports, which stalls or backfires

rules.rule: Identify what specifically motivates this audience (e.g., financial return, market share, efficiency, mission impact, recognition) and frame the emphasized benefit in those terms rather than using one generic value proposition for everyone.
rules.applies_when: always, when stating the benefit of the recommendation
rules.check: The stated primary benefit matches a motivation documented for this specific audience, not a generic list of benefits.
rules.prevents: a pitch that lists benefits the audience doesn't actually care about while missing the one they do

rules.rule: Engage both the audience's reasoning and emotions rather than logic alone, and calibrate the ratio to audience type: technical/analytical audiences need emotional framing concentrated mainly in the open and close around an analytical core, while audiences facing a sensitive or emotionally charged topic need more emotional context around fewer analytical proof points.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: The deck includes some emotional/narrative framing even for analytical audiences, and includes solid analytical evidence even when the topic is emotionally charged; the ratio shifts with audience type.
rules.prevents: losing analytical audiences to excess emotion, or losing emotionally invested audiences to a purely clinical argument

merged_from.rule: Pair analytical or quantitative evidence with human-impact or emotionally resonant material (a story, image, or named outcome), especially when the audience includes non-technical decision-makers.
merged_from.check: major claims have both a logical/quantitative support and a human-relevance element, not quantitative support only

rules.rule: Before finalizing, test comprehension with a stand-in reviewer who matches the target audience's lack of specialist background or organizational context, and use their confusion or surprise to identify what needs clearer explanation.
rules.applies_when: in the qa stage, before a draft is considered final
rules.check: A reviewer without the presenter's specialist/insider context has reviewed the draft and their points of confusion have been addressed.
rules.prevents: author blindness to jargon or assumed context that the real audience won't have

rules.rule: In the opening, explicitly state why the topic matters to this specific audience — tie it to a change, risk, or decision in their situation — rather than assuming relevance is self-evident.
rules.applies_when: always, in the opening section
rules.check: The opening names a consequence or decision relevant to this audience, not just background facts about the topic.
rules.prevents: an opening that conveys information without giving the audience a reason to care

merged_from.rule: Frame the core problem or claim in terms of its specific relevance to the audience's own situation, timing, and decisions — or, for a routine update, what the new information now lets them do — rather than its importance to the presenter internally.
merged_from.check: Does the claim explain why this matters to the audience's own goals or constraints right now, or only why it mattered internally to produce the deck?

rules.rule: Assume audience members with lower domain expertise will overestimate their own understanding of technical or market claims, and explain key technical claims explicitly with concrete evidence rather than waiting for the audience to signal confusion.
rules.applies_when: audience includes members with lower domain expertise on a technical or specialized claim
rules.check: Technical claims aimed at less-expert audience members are explained with concrete supporting evidence rather than stated as self-evident.
rules.prevents: investor overconfidence in their own understanding, leading to incomplete diligence or misjudged risk

rules.rule: Define the desired outcome or end-state in specific, measurable terms — not a vague aspiration — including what the audience's role in reaching it looks like.
rules.applies_when: defining the objective of a problem-solving or persuasive deck
rules.check: The stated desired outcome includes a concrete, checkable end-state (a number, a specific action, a defined state), not just a general direction.
rules.prevents: ambiguous objectives that make it impossible to tell whether the recommendation actually works

rules.rule: For small, working-meeting audiences (e.g., board meetings), favor a sparser deck that supports discussion, reserving detailed material for the appendix; reserve dense, self-contained treatment for large-group or one-way audiences (e.g., a conference pitch).
rules.applies_when: presentation setting is known to be a small working meeting versus a large one-way presentation
rules.check: Board/small-meeting decks are sparse with detail pushed to appendix; large-audience decks are more self-contained.
rules.prevents: a dense one-way deck that shuts down discussion in a small working meeting, or a sparse deck that leaves a large passive audience without enough context

rules.rule: When the presentation's purpose is primarily educational or explanatory (e.g., briefing a scientific advisory board) rather than a fundraising pitch, favor demonstrated reasoning, evidence, and open questions over promotional pitch techniques.
rules.applies_when: audience purpose is advisory/educational rather than a funding decision
rules.check: Advisory-audience decks lead with reasoning and evidence rather than the persuasive framing typical of a pitch.
rules.prevents: treating an expert advisory audience like a sales prospect, which damages credibility

rules.rule: Use humor, metaphor, or other creative devices only when the specific audience and setting will welcome them. Never open with humor; place it after credibility is established. Avoid it entirely in small, formal, or institutional settings (LP, board, investor) unless receptiveness is documented. Any humor must be embedded in a substantive point so the content lands even if the joke doesn't, must relate to the topic, and must never rely on stereotypes, sensitive topics, or mockery of anyone present.
rules.applies_when: considering humor, metaphor, or other creative/unconventional devices
rules.check: Humor, if present, is absent from the opening, absent from formal or institutional decks without documented receptiveness, embedded in a substantive point, on topic, and free of stereotypes or mockery.
rules.prevents: awkward silence or perceived tone-deafness that damages credibility with a serious audience

merged_from.rule: If using humor, embed it within a substantive point so the content still lands even if the joke doesn't.
merged_from.check: Does humorous content remain part of a substantive point rather than standing alone as a non-sequitur?

merged_from.rule: Keep any humor relevant to the topic, and avoid humor built on stereotypes, slurs, political, religious, or racial material, or mockery of the audience.
merged_from.check: confirm every instance of humor relates to the presentation's topic, and none relies on stereotypes, slurs, political/religious/racial content, or mockery of anyone in the room

curation: Absorbs NAR-48 and FAIL-28 into one humor rule. Resolves the humor-timing tension in favor of alley-craft and abela-advanced (two authors) over reynolds-zen (one), since credibility risk is highest in the opening. Brand profiles may override this rule.

rules.rule: State explicitly in the opening what background knowledge the presentation assumes the audience already has, so audience members lacking it can calibrate their expectations.
rules.applies_when: audience has mixed or unknown prior-knowledge levels
rules.check: The opening or an early slide states the assumed prerequisite knowledge.
rules.prevents: audience frustration from feeling unprepared without knowing why they're lost

rules.rule: Use an assertion-evidence slide structure (explicit claim plus supporting technical evidence) for technically expert audiences, and a sparser image- or story-led structure for general or non-technical audiences.
rules.applies_when: choosing overall slide structure/layout approach
rules.check: Slide structure choice (assertion-evidence vs. image-led) matches the stated audience's technical expertise.
rules.prevents: a structure-audience mismatch that reduces clarity for either experts or generalists

rules.rule: Order the narrative by the sequence of questions the audience will naturally ask (why this matters, what was found, then how/methodology), not by the chronological sequence in which the work was performed.
rules.applies_when: always, when ordering sections in the outline
rules.check: Methodology/process detail appears after significance and findings are established, not before.
rules.prevents: audience confusion or lost interest from a deck that opens with methods before establishing why it matters

rules.rule: Frame the recommendation as consistent with the audience's own previously stated commitments, strategy, or prior decisions, since audiences are more receptive to proposals aligned with positions they've already taken.
rules.applies_when: the audience has known prior related commitments or stated positions
rules.check: The deck explicitly connects the recommendation to a specific prior position or commitment of the audience.
rules.prevents: audience resistance rooted in perceived inconsistency with their own stated views

rules.rule: Frame the ask so it preserves the audience's willingness to engage again in the future — tone and credibility intact — rather than optimizing only for winning this immediate decision.
rules.applies_when: the audience relationship is likely to continue regardless of this decision's outcome (e.g., LP relationships, board relationships)
rules.check: The deck's tone and requests don't corner or embarrass the audience if they decline, and credibility-damaging claims are avoided.
rules.prevents: winning one ask at the cost of damaging an ongoing relationship

rules.rule: Distill the material into a single one-sentence thesis, decision, or belief the audience should leave with before sequencing the deck; every section and slide must trace back to it without a logical gap, and anything that doesn't advance it gets cut, shortened, or moved to notes/appendix.
rules.applies_when: always, before and during outlining
rules.check: Can the whole deck be summarized in one sentence? Can every top-level section be shown to advance that sentence? Would removing any section weaken the case rather than just shorten it?
rules.prevents: unfocused, multi-threaded decks where the audience can't identify the ask or takeaway, padded with tangential material

rules.rule: Default to stating the core thesis, recommendation, or answer before the supporting argument, at both the deck level and within individual sections. Delay it only when: the audience doesn't yet accept that the underlying problem exists (build the case first, put the recommendation at the end of that case), the claim is complex, controversial, or counter-intuitive enough that stating it first would get it reflexively rejected, or the section's purpose is inspirational/vision-building rather than a tactical decision, where withholding the resolution sustains motivating tension.
rules.applies_when: default for all decks and sections; exceptions listed above must be a deliberate, recorded choice, not an accident of drafting order
rules.check: Does the opening or section lead with the claim, unless one of the three exceptions is explicitly recorded? For time-constrained decision audiences and negative or contrary findings, does the recommendation or finding still appear early rather than being saved as a reveal?
rules.prevents: decision-makers losing the thread waiting for the ask, or an unmotivated claim being rejected before its support is heard
rules.note: Precedence among ordering rules: the deck-level thesis is always stated in the opening or executive summary (this rule, NAR-38). Body sections follow AUD-15 (order by audience trust and disposition). An individual counterintuitive claim follows NAR-03 (surface the assumption, then evidence, then the assertion). The vision-building exception is executed through NAR-07. Absorbs NAR-02.

merged_from.rule: Make the opening slide's claim maximally specific and state the actual thesis immediately, rather than describing the deck's mechanics, the speaker, or a generic subject area.
merged_from.check: Does the opening state the concrete thesis or subject within the first sentence, avoiding phrasing like 'Today I'll talk about...'?

rules.rule: For a claim that is complex, controversial, or contradicts a likely audience assumption, name or surface that assumption and present the supporting evidence before stating the assertion prominently, rather than leading with the assertion.
rules.applies_when: an individual claim is counter-intuitive or high-friction relative to what the audience likely believes
rules.check: For claims flagged as counter-intuitive, does the sequence show evidence or the expected assumption before the assertion is stated?
rules.prevents: audiences reflexively dismissing a claim, or failing to register why a counter-intuitive finding matters, before they've evaluated its support

rules.rule: Structure the overall narrative as situation, then complication, then resolution, repeating complication-resolution cycles as needed, rather than as a flat list of topics or an agenda.
rules.applies_when: always, for the deck's overall arc
rules.check: Can each section be labeled situation, complication, or resolution in sequence? Is there no section organized as a standalone topic disconnected from this arc?
rules.prevents: disconnected, presenter-logic ordering that audiences can't follow or retain; topic-based decks that read as a report rather than an argument
rules.note: Empirical support from duarte-datastory: narrative-structured data is recalled and acted on at higher rates than analytically organized data.

rules.rule: Open the presentation with a situation the audience already accepts as true, a complication that disrupts it, and the question that follows from both, then state the thesis immediately afterward as the direct answer, before other supporting detail.
rules.applies_when: always, for the deck's opening
rules.check: Do the opening slides establish an accepted baseline, name what changed or is wrong, and state or clearly imply one question — with the thesis stated right after, not buried under background?
rules.prevents: openings that state facts without motivating why the audience should care, or that bury the point under throat-clearing

merged_from.rule: Limit the opening situation/complication to facts the audience already knows or will immediately accept as true; do not introduce new or debatable information before stating the main claim.
merged_from.check: Every statement in the opening is verifiable as something the stated audience already believes or knows; no new evidence appears before the main claim.

merged_from.rule: Keep the opening or context-setting section free of exhibits or evidence that needs proving — use only statements the audience would already accept as true.
merged_from.check: no chart, data point, or citation appears before the core claim is introduced; the opening contains only background the audience would agree with unprompted

rules.rule: At the section or claim level, write the claim so it implicitly raises a specific question, and establish the need or gap that motivates it before presenting the evidence; place that evidence immediately beneath the claim in an order that visibly builds toward it, answering exactly that question rather than listing loosely related facts.
rules.applies_when: always, at the section/claim level
rules.check: For each claim, identify the question a skeptical reader would ask; confirm the following evidence answers exactly that question in sequence, not as a set of facts whose relevance was never established.
rules.prevents: evidence that feels arbitrary or imposed because its relevance to the claim above it was never established

rules.rule: In persuasive sections aimed at motivating change, present the audience's current or problematic state before the proposed future state, using the contrast to drive engagement; when the goal is to inspire or shift belief rather than secure an immediate tactical decision, delay the full resolution rather than stating it immediately, to sustain motivating tension.
rules.applies_when: persuasive or vision/opportunity sections; the delayed-resolution variant applies specifically when the purpose is inspirational rather than a time-constrained decision ask
rules.check: Does current-state/problem content appear before future-state/solution content? In vision-purpose sections, is the resolution developed rather than front-loaded?
rules.prevents: a flattened, unmotivating narrative that states the conclusion before the audience has felt the stakes
rules.note: Contrasting current vs. future state has measured engagement effects (duarte-resonate); pairs with the default-lead-with-claim rule's vision exception.

rules.rule: Limit any list, grouping, or the top-level outline to roughly three to five items (ideally three to four major sections); when a natural set would exceed four or five items, regroup it into two or three categories rather than presenting a flat long list, and don't add hierarchy levels beyond what the underlying logic requires.
rules.applies_when: structuring the outline's main sections or any list/grouping of related items
rules.check: Count top-level sections (flag more than four); count items in any list or grouping level (flag more than four or five, or a hierarchy level that exists only to break up space rather than clarify logic).
rules.prevents: cognitive overload and reduced retention from too many ungrouped items or overly deep hierarchies

rules.rule: Organize supporting claims hierarchically under the main message into non-overlapping, collectively exhaustive categories, and open each major section with a brief overview before its supporting detail.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: Do supporting claims sort into distinct categories without overlap or gaps? Does each major section begin with a one-line overview before detail?
rules.prevents: flat, ungrouped evidence lists that force sequential processing and hide the relationship between parts and the whole

merged_from.rule: When grouping a list of claims, problems, or causes, sort them into mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive categories before deciding their order.
merged_from.check: re-sort the list into categories by type; flag any item that belongs in two categories or in none

merged_from.rule: Evidence grouped under one claim must share a single category, must not contain items that don't fit it, and must not be missing an obvious category a reader would expect — and the claim itself should make clear whether that evidence set is complete.
merged_from.check: can every item in the group be labeled with the same plural noun? does an obvious category of supporting evidence seem to be missing? does the claim signal whether the grouped evidence is sufficient?

rules.rule: Choose an ordering scheme deliberately based on the nature of each section's content — chronological for processes, spatial for physical or system layouts, thematic or logical grouping for argumentative or diagnostic content — apply it consistently within that group, and never default to the order the underlying work or research happened.
rules.applies_when: ordering content within any section or grouping
rules.check: Does a non-process, argument-driven section follow chronological/work order instead of a logical or thematic grouping? Within one grouping, is a single consistent scheme (chronological, structural, or degree-of-importance) used throughout rather than mixed?
rules.prevents: confusing or arbitrary ordering that obscures the logical relationships between points, or sequences driven by data availability rather than logic

rules.rule: When the main assertion requires building acceptance rather than being self-evident, sequence supporting claims as a deductive chain where accepting each one moves the audience closer to the next; more generally, keep any single level of support to one logic type — either parallel/inductive grouping or deductive chaining — never mixed within that level.
rules.applies_when: constructing the supporting logic under any single claim
rules.check: Does each supporting claim depend on or build from the one before it, or could the claims be reordered arbitrarily without loss? For each level of support, is the logic purely inductive or purely deductive, not a mix?
rules.prevents: audiences rejecting the conclusion because a necessary intermediate step was skipped, or confused reasoning where parallel examples and chained argument are indistinguishable

rules.rule: Mark transitions between major sections explicitly: use connective language that states the logical relationship (e.g., 'but', 'so', 'therefore') and echo a specific term or claim from the section just closed rather than announcing the mechanical act of moving on.
rules.applies_when: moving between major sections
rules.check: Does each transition include a phrase or cue stating how the next section relates to the previous one, naming a specific carried-over idea rather than phrasing like 'next, let's look at'?
rules.prevents: audiences losing track of how sections relate, or a mechanical, inert thread between sections

rules.rule: Open with a brief, substantive hook: an unexpected but relevant fact, a premise the audience already accepts, a story, or a challenge to conventional wisdom. It should establish relevance before the core message, land within the first few minutes of live delivery, and be factually accurate and explicitly connected to the core message. Keep the opening to roughly 10% of the deck or less, and don't open on process or an agenda. Humor is not an opening device (see AUD-34).
rules.applies_when: always, for the opening
rules.check: Does the opening establish relevance in one or two slides (or the first few minutes live) before moving to the core message, without stalling on setup or opening on a topic list?
rules.prevents: a cold, over-long, or process-first opening that fails to motivate the audience or delays the main point

merged_from.rule: An opening hook built on a personal story or a surprising fact must be factually accurate, genuinely novel if framed as new, and explicitly tied to the deck's core message rather than serving as general background.
merged_from.check: the story or fact is verifiable, its novelty claim (if any) is current, and the connection to the core message is stated explicitly rather than left implicit

curation: Absorbs EVD-72 (hook accuracy). Removes humor from acceptable opening hooks to resolve the NAR humor-timing tension.

rules.rule: For decks with more than about three major sections, help the audience track structure, calibrated to genre: in research or technical presentations, where material complexity makes orientation valuable, include a visible roadmap slide naming the sections early; in persuasive or pitch decks, skip a formal, repeatedly-referenced agenda slide and instead follow the opening hook with a brief, lightweight preview of where the narrative is going.
rules.applies_when: decks with more than three major sections or topics
rules.check: In research/technical decks, does an early slide map the sections? In persuasive/pitch decks, is there no upfront agenda slide the deck returns to as topic markers, but a brief preview after the hook instead?
rules.prevents: audience disorientation in complex material, or narrative momentum breaking into a mechanical topic list in a persuasive deck
rules.note: Reconciles alley-craft's research-context roadmap recommendation with abela/reynolds/zelazny's caution against agenda-first openings in persuasive decks by genre; kosslyn/mayer support explicit structure cues for longer, complex decks generally.

rules.rule: Place the most important claim or material at the beginning or end of a section, and of the deck as a whole — putting the single strongest point in the opening and another strong point in the close — rather than burying critical points in the middle, where audience memory is weakest.
rules.applies_when: always, sequencing content within any section or across the whole deck
rules.check: Within each section and across the deck, does the most important point land in the first or last third rather than the middle?
rules.prevents: key evidence going unnoticed or forgotten due to primacy/recency effects in audience memory

rules.rule: If the main conclusion is negative or contrary to what the audience expects, state it early rather than revealing it as a surprise at the end, then frame the remainder of the deck around implications and next steps.
rules.applies_when: the deck's conclusion is negative or contrary to audience expectations (e.g., an underperforming metric in an LP update)
rules.check: If the headline finding is negative, does it appear early rather than being withheld until the final slides?
rules.prevents: audiences feeling misled by a late, unexpected negative reveal

rules.rule: End with an explicit, unambiguous statement of the recommended action, framed around what happens next rather than a mere recap, and signal clearly that the close has arrived; for decks requiring stakeholder sign-off or implementation, sequence the close as a summary of conclusions, a restated recommendation, an action plan with owners/timeline/budget, an explicit request for agreement, and confirmation of next steps — and, when the ask concludes a vision or opportunity narrative, depict the transformed future state at a higher, more concrete register than the opening.
rules.applies_when: always, for the closing; the five-part sequence applies specifically when implementation or sign-off is required
rules.check: Does the final section state a specific action or decision, not just a recap? Where implementation is required, are all five elements present? Where the close is vision-driven, does it depict a concrete resulting future state rather than restating the status quo?
rules.prevents: audiences finishing unsure what they're being asked to do, or a flat close that fails to compel commitment

rules.rule: Proactively address the strongest objections and alternative approaches a knowledgeable audience would expect to see considered — state which alternatives were evaluated and why each was rejected, evaluate every alternative against the same explicit goal criteria rather than against each other, and explicitly compare the recommendation to inaction or the status quo. When addressing several objections, order them from hardest to easiest to resolve. Don't manufacture or introduce alternatives the audience hasn't raised and wouldn't expect, unless the goal itself is genuinely ambiguous.
rules.applies_when: always, when credible objections or alternatives exist, or when presenting a competitive landscape or build-vs-buy analysis
rules.check: Does the deck name rejected alternatives with reasons, evaluated against stated criteria? Is inaction addressed directly? Are addressed objections ordered hardest-to-easiest? Is any introduced alternative one the audience would plausibly expect, not a strawman?
rules.prevents: objections surfacing unaddressed in discussion, or a false-choice comparison that doesn't test options against what matters, or a defensive-feeling deck arguing against concerns nobody raised

merged_from.rule: Surface genuine, serious objections or competing evidence to a recommendation and rebut them substantively; route complex or unlikely objections to the appendix instead of the main flow.
merged_from.check: known serious objections appear with a substantive rebuttal; low-likelihood or tangential objections sit in appendix, not main slides

merged_from.rule: For audiences known to weigh options thoroughly before deciding (e.g., diligence-driven investors), explicitly show the alternatives considered and why they were rejected, not just the chosen recommendation.
merged_from.check: A slide or notes section names at least one rejected alternative and the reason it was rejected.

rules.rule: Close each major section with a one- or two-sentence summary of its key conclusion before moving to the next section.
rules.applies_when: always, for decks with distinct major sections
rules.check: Does each major section end with an explicit restatement of its takeaway, not just a transition?
rules.prevents: audiences losing or forgetting a section's point once several more slides have passed

rules.rule: Write slide titles as terse, direct statements of each slide's point rather than labels, so that reading only the titles in sequence — without any other content — tells a coherent, self-contained account of the argument from opening to close.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: Extract every slide title/headline in order and read them alone; do they form a coherent narrative rather than a list of topic labels?
rules.prevents: a deck that only makes sense reading full content line-by-line, and drifting section-to-section logic that goes unnoticed

merged_from.rule: Read every slide title in the deck in sequence, independent of body content, and confirm they form a coherent, logically progressing argument on their own.
merged_from.check: Extract all titles into a list and read them top to bottom without slide bodies; does the narrative make sense and does each title follow logically from the last?

rules.rule: Introduce foundational concepts, terminology, and load-bearing assumptions before the claims or processes that depend on them, framed in terms of how they will be used later; place them in or immediately after the opening unless they warrant their own clearly-connected section.
rules.applies_when: the audience may lack domain background needed for later claims, or the work depends on non-obvious assumptions
rules.check: Is every technical term or concept defined before its first substantive use? Are major assumptions stated near the opening rather than surfacing later without warning?
rules.prevents: audience confusion from encountering unexplained terms, mechanisms, or load-bearing assumptions mid-argument

rules.rule: Distribute complex, technical, or multi-stage content across multiple sequential slides, each focused on one concept, step, or aspect, with a clear break between segments, rather than compressing it onto one dense slide.
rules.applies_when: content involves a sequential process, workflow, or multi-part system, or is otherwise complex/technical for the audience
rules.check: Does a multi-step process or complex system appear across separate, sequential slides rather than crammed into one? Does each segment address one primary concept before advancing?
rules.prevents: audience overload or missed relationships in complex, multi-part content

merged_from.rule: When explaining a multi-step or multi-part process to a non-expert audience, devote one slide to each major step rather than compressing the whole process onto a single slide.
merged_from.check: No single slide attempts to explain more than one major step or component of the process.

rules.rule: In explanatory or technical sections for a general or investor audience, sequence content as concept explanation, then a worked example, then application; don't open a section with an unsolved problem before the explanation, and interleave examples with practice rather than grouping all examples before all exercises.
rules.applies_when: explanatory or technical sections for a general or investor audience, not specialized teaching contexts with instructor-guided problem-solving
rules.check: Does concept explanation precede its worked example, which precedes application? Are examples and practice interleaved rather than block-separated?
rules.prevents: cognitive overload from an unexplained opening problem, and inefficient learning from block-separated examples and practice

merged_from.rule: For audiences new to a topic, establish key terms and a concrete worked example before showing a complex diagram or abstract principle that depends on them.
merged_from.check: the deck or section introduces foundational terms/concepts and at least one concrete example before the detailed diagram or abstract claim that relies on them

rules.rule: When using multiple examples to illustrate one shared principle, place them on the same or adjacent slides and explicitly prompt the audience to compare them.
rules.applies_when: using multiple examples or case studies to establish one shared pattern
rules.check: Do comparable examples sit contiguously, with a cue directing the audience to compare them?
rules.prevents: the audience treating each example in isolation and missing the underlying pattern

rules.rule: When presenting analysis of a genuinely ambiguous or complex problem, acknowledge that multiple legitimate analytical approaches exist rather than forcing a single method as the only valid one.
rules.applies_when: genuine methodological ambiguity exists (e.g., competing valid scientific or analytical approaches)
rules.check: Where more than one credible method or framing exists in the source material, does the deck or notes acknowledge it?
rules.prevents: tunnel vision that hides real alternative approaches an informed audience would expect addressed

rules.rule: Where the deck offers expandable, appendix, or optional navigation, keep the default path following the main argument's order, mark supplementary content clearly as optional and cuttable under time pressure, and don't let material required for later comprehension be marked skippable for audiences new to the subject.
rules.applies_when: the deck or notes/appendix layer has expandable or skippable content
rules.check: Does the default forward path match the intended argument order? Are appendix/expandable items visibly marked optional? Is at least one section identified as cuttable without creating a logical gap, and are foundational slides protected from being marked skippable for novice audiences?
rules.prevents: audiences skipping material required for later comprehension, or being forced to cut load-bearing content under time pressure because nothing was pre-designated as optional

rules.rule: Organize appendix or leave-behind material meant to be read non-sequentially as a grouping/MECE structure, not as a deductive chain that only works if read start-to-finish.
rules.applies_when: appendix content, leave-behind documents, or expandable/notes layers meant for selective reading
rules.check: Can appendix sections be read in any order without losing their meaning?
rules.prevents: appendix material that is unreadable or unpersuasive when a reader skips to the one section they care about

rules.rule: For decks longer than about 10 slides or intended as leave-behinds, include a table of contents with page numbers, finalized only after content and slide order are set.
rules.applies_when: decks longer than roughly 10 slides, or meant to be read/referenced independently
rules.check: Does a long or standalone deck have a TOC with accurate page numbers reflecting the final slide order?
rules.prevents: readers unable to navigate or grasp the document's structure at a glance, or a TOC with stale page numbers

rules.rule: When a deck must serve both live delivery and standalone reading, maintain two versions — a delivery-optimized one and a more complete standalone one — and make the live-delivery path lighter and more selective than the reading version, since listeners cannot reread or skip ahead.
rules.applies_when: the same deck must be both presented live and sent or read independently
rules.check: Do separate live and standalone versions exist? Is the live path lighter in claims-per-minute than the reading/appendix version?
rules.prevents: compromising either live delivery effectiveness or standalone clarity by forcing one version to serve both purposes

rules.rule: For high-stakes decisions, distribute a self-contained written briefing before the live session and use the live session as guided discussion of that material rather than a first read-through.
rules.applies_when: high-stakes decision presentations (e.g., board or LP decisions) where the deck will be read in advance
rules.check: Is a complete version of the deck or memo sent before the session, with the live agenda framed as discussion/Q&A rather than first exposure?
rules.prevents: wasting live meeting time delivering information the audience could absorb faster by reading beforehand

rules.rule: For research or scientific presentations, follow the field's expected sequence — background/context, hypothesis or research question, methodology, results, conclusions, and future directions.
rules.applies_when: research or scientific presentations
rules.check: Does context and hypothesis precede methodology, and methodology precede results?
rules.prevents: audience frustration from violated genre expectations, and results that feel unmotivated

rules.rule: When a plan has multiple objectives, make the causal relationship between them explicit — which are means to another, which are complementary, which are independent — rather than listing them as isolated bullets.
rules.applies_when: roadmap, milestone, or multi-objective strategy sections
rules.check: Is each objective's relationship to the others stated or diagrammed, not left for the audience to infer?
rules.prevents: audiences left to guess how milestones or goals depend on or support one another

rules.rule: Give the deck a visible arc — setup, development, resolution — connecting the central claim to concrete stakes or examples; in decks longer than a few sections, distribute several peaks of resolution or emphasis that each build toward the next, rather than saving all impact for one climax at the end.
rules.applies_when: always, when shaping the overall narrative; the multiple-peaks guidance applies specifically to presentations longer than a few sections
rules.check: Do the deck's sections map onto a setup/development/resolution progression, with at least one concrete example or stake present? In longer decks, is there more than one moment of payoff distributed through the body?
rules.prevents: a sequence of disconnected facts that fails to build toward a conclusion, or audience disengagement after an early resolution with no momentum left for the rest of the deck

rules.rule: When data includes both a decline and a recovery, show the worse/lower figures before the better ones to sharpen the sense of improvement.
rules.applies_when: presenting trend data that includes both a decline and a recovery period
rules.check: Do worse numbers appear before better numbers when both exist in the narrative sequence?
rules.prevents: understating the magnitude of improvement by leading with the better numbers

rules.rule: When a single negative metric has multiple distinct underlying causes, address each cause separately in the narrative rather than treating it as one undifferentiated problem.
rules.applies_when: a single outcome (e.g., churn, a missed target) is driven by more than one distinct type of barrier
rules.check: Are multiple distinct causes each given their own explanation and, where relevant, their own response, rather than merged into one generic explanation?
rules.prevents: recommendations that address only one of several real barriers, leaving the problem unresolved

rules.rule: For senior or time-constrained audiences, or supporting documents longer than a few pages, open with (or include) a short executive summary structured in three parts: the current situation, the specific measurable change required (with direction), and the outcome if the recommended action is taken — with the action addressing the root cause and an explicit causal link from action to the required metric — so the full story is graspable from that section alone.
rules.applies_when: presentations to senior leaders/investors, or supporting documents longer than a few pages
rules.check: Can you identify a situation statement, a specific required change in a named metric with direction, and a proposed action with an explicit causal path to that metric, all within a section short enough to stand alone?
rules.prevents: senior audiences having to sit through the entire deck to find the recommendation, vague problem statements, and recommendations that treat symptoms rather than root causes

merged_from.rule: In a slidedoc, include an executive-summary page near the front stating the key recommendation or finding in full sentences before the supporting detail.
merged_from.check: An executive-summary page near the beginning states the conclusion, not just a topic preview

rules.rule: If using a recurring metaphor or theme, apply it consistently across the deck rather than switching metaphors for the same underlying idea.
rules.applies_when: the deck uses a metaphorical or thematic frame
rules.check: Does the same motif reappear at multiple points to reinforce the same idea, rather than being replaced?
rules.prevents: audience confusion from competing or inconsistent symbolic references

rules.rule: Include one standout, memorable moment — an evocative image, a striking statistic, or a concise story — that directly crystallizes the core message, rather than serving as unrelated entertainment.
rules.applies_when: the deck needs to be remembered and discussed after the meeting ends
rules.check: Is there one identifiable moment a reader would repeat afterward, and does it directly support the core message?
rules.prevents: a forgettable deck, or a memorable moment that distracts from the point

rules.rule: When a deck is built from a larger source document, extract key findings and implications rather than reproducing exhaustive methodology; in data-heavy or recurring-report sections, open with the story-driven insight before comprehensive data, moving tables and reference material to an appendix.
rules.applies_when: the deck is derived from a longer document or report, or covers a data-heavy/recurring-metrics section
rules.check: Does the deck lead with findings and implications, with exhaustive detail moved to an appendix rather than occupying the primary slide?
rules.prevents: an overwhelmed audience, diluted persuasive impact, and analytical work whose conclusion never surfaces

rules.rule: State explicitly which topics are out of scope and why when the audience might reasonably expect them to be included, and when the deck offers less than a complete solution, state explicitly what level of contribution it offers (a partial solution, defining the solution space, or clarifying the problem).
rules.applies_when: the deck's scope omits content the audience might assume is covered, or is narrower than the full problem domain
rules.check: If an expected topic is absent, does the deck note the exclusion and reason? Does the deck state what it will and will not resolve, rather than implying full resolution by omission?
rules.prevents: audience confusion or suspicion about unexplained gaps, and disappointment from a partial solution perceived as inadequate because expectations weren't set

rules.rule: For recommendations that shift resources or benefits between stakeholder groups, frame the narrative at the organization- or portfolio-wide level, presenting the problem, alternatives, and evaluation criteria before the recommendation.
rules.applies_when: the recommendation reallocates capital or benefit between stakeholder groups (e.g., across portfolio companies or funds)
rules.check: Is the recommendation framed from a portfolio-wide perspective, with criteria stated before the recommendation, rather than from one stakeholder's point of view?
rules.prevents: loss of buy-in from stakeholders who perceive the deck as favoring one group

rules.rule: When source material spans multiple distinct problems, either focus the deck on the single most significant one or genuinely aggregate them into one coherent combined problem, rather than listing several unrelated issues.
rules.applies_when: source material contains multiple separate issues
rules.check: Does the deck address one clearly primary problem, or a genuinely combined framing, rather than a scattered list?
rules.prevents: a scattered, unfocused presentation

rules.rule: When the goal is collaborative exploration without a settled solution, state upfront that the deck is exploratory rather than a predetermined recommendation, and present a small number of critical questions with multiple preliminary answers.
rules.applies_when: no clear solution exists and the goal is collaborative problem framing rather than a decision ask
rules.check: Does the deck explicitly signal it is exploratory, and present multiple candidate answers rather than one fixed recommendation?
rules.prevents: audience confusion about whether they are being asked to decide or to explore

rules.rule: For recurring status or update presentations, open by briefly reestablishing prior context and progress, then organize the body around what newly requires the audience's thinking or action, moving unchanged status information to an appendix.
rules.applies_when: recurring update presentations (e.g., quarterly LP updates, portfolio reviews)
rules.check: Does the opening briefly restate prior progress before new content? Does the body focus on what changed or newly needs a decision, with static detail in an appendix?
rules.prevents: audience confusion from missing context, and bloated updates diluted by unchanged detail

merged_from.rule: In recurring update presentations to the same audience, lead with new or changed findings and minimize repeating established facts.
merged_from.check: the evidence selected is weighted toward what changed since the last update, not a full restatement of known background

rules.rule: Size total slide count and depth to the available delivery time — as a default guideline, roughly one slide per two minutes — and for decisions in a fixed time slot (investor pitch, board approval), cap the core narrative at about 10 slides / 20 minutes, cutting or moving overflow to appendix or notes rather than padding or rushing; within that budget, allocate slides or visuals per idea according to its complexity, not an even or arbitrary split.
rules.applies_when: always for time-boxed live presentations; the 10-slide/20-minute cap applies specifically to investor, board, or other fixed-slot decision meetings
rules.check: Does estimated delivery time fit the meeting's time box, with overflow detail in appendix/notes rather than inflating the core deck? Within the deck, are complex ideas given more visuals than simple ones, rather than a uniform allocation?
rules.prevents: presenters running out of time before the ask, audiences reading ahead of a rushed presenter, over-simplified treatment of complex claims, or padded treatment of simple ones
rules.note: Sizing follows from the meeting's fixed time box, not from treating slide count as a quality metric in itself.

rules.rule: In presentations or sessions longer than roughly 15-20 minutes, vary the delivery format across sections — mixing data, story, demonstration, or a second speaker — rather than sustaining one format throughout.
rules.applies_when: presentations or sessions longer than roughly 15-20 minutes
rules.check: Do at least two distinct formats or pacing changes appear across the deck?
rules.prevents: monotonous, single-format sessions that lose audience attention over time

rules.rule: Before building detailed slides, draft and pressure-test a condensed version of the narrative — a roughly three-minute spoken narration, or a skeleton reviewed in a five-to-ten-minute discussion — covering situation, complication, resolution, and ask, and use it to check the logic holds before investing in slide detail.
rules.applies_when: before moving from message_model/outline into detailed slide_spec work
rules.check: Does a stand-alone narration or skeleton exist that was reviewed for logical soundness, independent of slides or visuals, before detailed slide work began?
rules.prevents: polished, detailed slides built on a narrative whose underlying logic was never checked, or costly restructuring discovered late

rules.rule: Develop the body of the argument using a deliberate range of evidence types — context, external comparisons, illustrative examples, data, consequences of inaction, alternatives considered, and benefits — rather than leaning on one type of evidence repeatedly.
rules.applies_when: developing the middle/body sections of the argument
rules.check: Across the body, can at least three distinct evidence types be identified, rather than one type repeated throughout?
rules.prevents: shallow argument development that relies on one form of proof

rules.rule: Organize problem-diagnosis sections around logical or causal frameworks — cause-effect chains, structural breakdowns, mutually exclusive categories — rather than functional departments or research workstreams, and sequence the deck's main sections to mirror problem, then diagnosis, then recommendation, with each recommendation tracing visibly back to a specific diagnostic finding.
rules.applies_when: structuring a diagnostic, root-cause, or problem-solving-driven analysis
rules.check: Do section headings name a cause-effect or structural logic rather than mirroring organizational functions or research workstreams? Does each recommendation trace back to a specific diagnostic finding?
rules.prevents: meandering diagnostic sections with no clear conclusion, and recommendations that appear unjustified because the diagnostic work isn't shown

rules.rule: Keep chronological or historical background confined to the introduction; structure the body around logical relationships between ideas, not a chronological recounting of events.
rules.applies_when: the deck includes historical or timeline background (e.g., company history, prior events)
rules.check: Do body sections argue by logical relationship rather than 'first this happened, then this happened'? Is chronology limited to the opening?
rules.prevents: a body that reads as a timeline recap instead of an argument, obscuring cause-and-effect
rules.note: Process descriptions in the body may still use chronological order where the content is a sequence (NAR-10). This rule targets recounting events in place of argument.

rules.rule: Match a section's internal logical structure to the type of question it answers: 'should we act' calls for weighing supporting versus opposing evidence, 'what should we do' calls for reasons or options leading to a choice, and 'how do we implement' calls for ordered execution steps.
rules.applies_when: structuring any section built around a specific question
rules.check: Identify the question the section answers; does its internal structure match that question type?
rules.prevents: mismatched structures that don't resolve the question posed

rules.rule: For an approval, funding, or investment ask, structure the argument in order: why the problem/opportunity is urgent, why the proposed solution addresses it, the financial justification, and any secondary benefits.
rules.applies_when: the deck includes a specific approval, funding, or investment request
rules.check: Does the ask section cover urgency, solution fit, financial case, and secondary benefits in that order, rather than jumping straight to a number?
rules.prevents: funding asks that leave decision-makers uncertain why the request is needed now or whether the numbers hold up

rules.rule: When proposing a change to an existing process, product, or strategy, show the current state and the proposed state side by side so the specific changes are explicit.
rules.applies_when: recommending a change to an existing process, system, or strategy
rules.check: Does the slide or section show both current and proposed states with differences highlighted?
rules.prevents: changes described in the abstract that leave the audience unsure what's actually different from today

merged_from.rule: When a claim proposes a change or recommendation, state the current condition explicitly before asserting the proposed direction, so the audience can see the contrast.
merged_from.check: Does the slide or its immediate context state what is true now before introducing what should change?

merged_from.rule: When recommending a process change, show the before-and-after process and give detailed evidence only for the steps that are broken and the specific fix, not the full process end-to-end.
merged_from.check: the explanation addresses only the steps where a problem exists and the specific change proposed, not routine unchanged steps

rules.rule: Never present a problem or risk without pairing it with a proposed response or mitigation in the same section.
rules.applies_when: raising a risk, weakness, or open problem anywhere in the deck
rules.check: Does every identified problem/risk have an accompanying response or plan in the same section?
rules.prevents: leaving the audience with an unresolved concern and no sense of how it will be handled

merged_from.rule: When a slide reveals a problem, risk, or negative trend, pair it with a specific recommendation or concrete next step the audience can take, rather than leaving the negative finding unresolved.
merged_from.check: Every slide stating a risk or negative finding is followed by or paired with a specific proposed response.

merged_from.rule: Don't frame a problem as severe or exceptional unless the deck follows through with a concrete, actionable response.
merged_from.check: wherever the draft raises alarm about a problem, confirm a specific, credible next step or mitigation appears nearby

rules.rule: For a deductive chain arguing toward an action, verify each link is airtight: that the stated cause is the root cause, that the current state is mapped to every criterion of the desired state, or that each named risk ties to a specific consequence — and nest further detail as grouping structures rather than chaining additional deductive steps.
rules.applies_when: persuasion sections that argue toward a recommended action via a chained cause-to-action, current-to-desired-state, or risk-to-consequence structure
rules.check: For each link in the chain, would removing it break the conclusion? Is a second deductive chain nested inside the first?
rules.prevents: recommendations that don't actually follow from the stated problem, or fragile logic chains that collapse if one link is challenged

merged_from.rule: In a deductive opening that argues from accepted premises to a recommendation, never introduce a claim that will need justification later in the deck.
merged_from.check: confirm every claim stated in the opening is either already established fact or uncontested, not something defended later

rules.rule: Size the introduction in proportion to how much context this specific audience actually needs, not to the length of the deck that follows.
rules.applies_when: writing the opening/introduction
rules.check: Is the opening brief for an audience already familiar with the situation, and more developed for an unfamiliar or complex topic, independent of total deck length?
rules.prevents: boring an expert audience with over-explanation, or confusing a new audience with too little setup

merged_from.rule: Skip an extended problem-framing or options-framing opening when the audience already knows the problem, its causes, or the decision options, and go straight to the recommendation.
merged_from.check: confirm during audience analysis whether key stakeholders already know this material; if so, the opening states the recommendation directly rather than re-deriving it

tensions.tension: Whether humor belongs in the opening itself: reynolds-zen lists relevant humor as one acceptable type of opening hook, on par with a surprising fact or personal story, while alley-craft and abela-advanced hold that humor should be placed after the opening, once the presenter's credibility is established, so a failed joke doesn't damage authority before it's earned. Both apply to the same context (live/presented decks) with no audience- or genre-based distinction given in the source material to separate them.
tensions.resolution: Humor is not an opening device. It comes after credibility is established, and only where AUD-34's conditions are met. Two authors (alley-craft, abela-advanced) against one (reynolds-zen), and the risk is concentrated in the opening.

rules.rule: Write every slide headline, and every heading placed over a group of claims, as a complete-sentence assertion of the actual conclusion or insight involved, in sentence case, never a topic label, category name, item count, or bare description of what was measured or grouped. Length is governed by CLM-05 (two lines maximum), not by a word target.
rules.applies_when: always, for any slide title, section heading, or heading that sits over multiple grouped claims
rules.check: Read the heading alone: does it assert something that could be true or false and identify the specific insight tying together what's beneath it, or does it merely name a subject, category, or count ('Retention', 'Three Findings', 'Retention by Cohort')?
rules.prevents: slides and sections whose point the audience must infer for themselves, and headings that function as filenames or placeholders instead of arguments
rules.note: Folds in a narrower rule about section/group headings naming a shared insight rather than a category label — same underlying principle as headline-as-assertion, just applied to grouped content.

merged_from.rule: Write each slide headline as a complete-sentence assertion of the slide's specific finding, not a topic label, in sentence-case capitalization, wrapped at phrase boundaries to no more than two lines.
merged_from.check: Is the headline a full sentence stating a claim? Does it exceed two lines or break mid-phrase? Is it sentence case rather than title case?

merged_from.rule: Write the header or summary line above any grouped set of supporting points to state the specific, shared insight or effect those points produce, not a generic category label; every item in the group should share one nameable type or contribute to the same specific effect.
merged_from.check: Can every item in the group be labeled with the same specific plural noun or shown to produce the same specific effect? Does the header state that insight rather than a generic word like 'Benefits' or 'Objectives'?

curation: Absorbs DSN-28 and NAR-12. Resolves the DSN headline-length tension: the 'six words per headline' figure contradicted this rule, which has support from 13 books across 11 authors, so it was dropped.

rules.rule: Limit each slide to one message, scoped tightly enough that it can be stated in a single sentence without joining two separable ideas with 'and'. Support that message with at most about two sub-points, and split the slide rather than compress it when content needs more. The claim should stay obvious at thumbnail size (the squint test).
rules.applies_when: always, when drafting or reviewing an individual slide
rules.check: Summarize the slide in one sentence. If it needs 'and' to join two claims, split it. Count sub-points (flag more than 2). Shrink the slide to thumbnail size and confirm the claim is still the most visible element.
rules.prevents: slides that carry two competing points, leaving the audience unsure which one to remember

merged_from.rule: Design each slide around a single main claim, statable in one sentence, with at most about two supporting sub-points; if content needs more, split it across additional slides rather than compressing it onto one, and make the claim legible even at a glance or from a distance (the squint test).
merged_from.check: Blur or shrink the slide thumbnail — is the main claim still obvious? Can the claim be stated in one sentence, and does every element support only that sentence? Count sub-points (flag more than ~2).

curation: Absorbs DSN-01, which stated the same rule plus the two-sub-point limit and squint test.

rules.rule: Settle on the slide's claim before selecting its evidence, then keep only the data, chart type, and emphasis that directly establish that claim — anything that doesn't help answer the question the claim raises should move to notes or be cut.
rules.applies_when: always, when assembling or reviewing a slide's supporting content
rules.check: For each piece of evidence on the slide, ask whether removing it would change how believable the claim is; if not, move it to notes or cut it.
rules.prevents: slides padded with tangential facts that dilute the claim, or evidence that doesn't actually establish what the headline asserts

rules.rule: Write claims at a level of specificity that only this slide's own evidence could support, using concrete, visualizable language rather than generic labels or abstractions.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: Could this exact claim be pasted onto a different slide with different evidence and still sound plausible? If so, sharpen it until it names the specific finding, number, or mechanism unique to this evidence.
rules.prevents: interchangeable, forgettable claims like 'strong results' or 'key challenges' that fail to differentiate one slide's evidence from another's

rules.rule: Cap slide headlines at two lines, trimming qualifiers and elaboration rather than letting the title wrap further.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: Render the title at the deck's actual title font size and column width; if it runs past two lines, cut words until it fits.
