rules.prevents: readers misjudging relative magnitude because panels use different scales, or a layout choice that obscures the intended comparison

merged_from.rule: When comparing several instances of similar data, render them as small multiples with identical frame size, scale, orientation, and labeling, varying only the data itself; keep chart axes, scales, and positions consistent from slide to slide across a sequence of related data slides rather than re-laying out each one independently.
merged_from.check: Confirm every panel in a comparison set shares the same bounding box, scale, and label style; compare axis position/scale across consecutive data slides for unexplained changes.

rules.rule: For composition data, use bar forms rather than pie charts: a single horizontal bar to show the parts of one whole, and 100%-stacked or grouped horizontal bars — not multiple side-by-side pies — to compare composition (including Likert-scale or survey data) across several items, groups, or time points. Label both edges of 100%-stacked bars and include or footnote the absolute totals behind each category's percentages so shares aren't read out of context, and keep the number of stacked series small, since stacked bars only let viewers reliably compare the bottom-anchored segment or the overall totals.
rules.applies_when: showing how components sum to a total, for one item or compared across several items or time points
rules.check: composition displays use bar forms, not pie charts; multi-group comparisons use consistent 100%-stacked or grouped bars rather than separate pies; absolute totals accompany percentage-only stacked bars; stacked-bar comparisons are limited to the bottom segment or totals
rules.prevents: inaccurate part-to-whole comparison, forcing the audience to compare wedge angles across disconnected pies, and comparisons that exceed what stacked bars can actually support

rules.rule: Use a scatterplot, not a grouped bar chart, to show the relationship between two continuous variables: distinguish multiple series by color plus a redundant shape or style cue, omit gridlines unless specific values must be read, add a fitted trend line when correlation strength is the point, make overlapping points visible through jitter or transparency, and avoid plotting multiple groups together unless they occupy visually distinct regions or their overlap is itself the message.
rules.applies_when: displaying bivariate continuous data where distribution, shape, correlation, or strength of relationship matters
rules.check: two-continuous-variable data appears as a scatterplot with color-plus-shape-coded series; gridlines are absent unless precision-reading is required; a trend line appears when correlation strength matters; overlapping points are distinguishable; multiple groups are either visually separated or their overlap is the stated message
rules.prevents: a poor overview of relationships, indistinguishable series, hidden point density, and unreadable mixed-group plots

rules.rule: Visually distinguish forecast or projected data from actual historical data on the same chart — a different line style, color, or shading — so the audience can't mistake a projection for a fact.
rules.applies_when: a chart mixes actual results with forecasts or projections, as in most financial or growth charts
rules.check: forecast segments use a visually distinct style (dashed line, different color, or shaded background) from actuals
rules.prevents: the audience treating a projection as already-achieved fact

rules.rule: Round displayed numbers to the precision that meaningfully distinguishes the values, stripping decimal places that imply more measurement accuracy than the data has, and use the same units of measurement and notation conventions for a given measurement type everywhere it appears across the deck.
rules.applies_when: labeling numeric values on axes, data points, or in text, especially across a deck mixing multiple data sources or units
rules.check: decimal precision shown matches the actual precision of the underlying measurement or estimate; units and notation are identical for the same measurement type everywhere it appears
rules.prevents: false precision that overstates how exact a figure actually is, and hidden unit errors that are especially costly with technical audiences

rules.rule: When a slide must show many individual categories, group them into labeled super-categories so the audience has a structure for interpreting the detail.
rules.applies_when: displaying a large number of individual categories (for example, many market or demographic segments)
rules.check: related categories are clustered under a labeled group rather than listed flat
rules.prevents: cognitive overload from an unstructured list of many items

rules.rule: Use a waterfall chart to show a starting value, the increments and decrements that build or break it down, and the resulting total — for example, a revenue or cash bridge. Use a slopegraph to show relative change and rank reshuffling across categories between exactly two points in time or conditions (before/after, baseline/current), but not when the categories' order carries fixed meaning that must be preserved, since a slopegraph re-sorts categories by value.
rules.applies_when: explaining what drove a change between two totals (waterfall), or comparing the same categories at exactly two points where ranking shifts matter (slopegraph)
rules.check: bridge-style changes between two totals use a waterfall rather than a stacked or simple bar; two-point comparisons use a slopegraph only where category order has no fixed meaning to protect
rules.prevents: losing visibility into which components drove an overall change, missing an efficient view of which categories moved most, and an unintended reordering that disrupts a sequence that must stay fixed

rules.rule: Translate raw scientific units and large abstract totals into terms the audience already has intuition for — a familiar comparison, reference quantity, or everyday unit — and don't let a raw number or a normalized chart (100%-stacked bars, percentage-only displays) stand without a comparison, benchmark, or the underlying absolute magnitude, adding it in a footnote if needed.
rules.applies_when: presenting a technical measurement, a large/unfamiliar quantity, or a scale-suppressing visualization to a non-specialist audience
rules.check: technical units and large numbers are accompanied by a relatable comparison or converted into a unit the audience already uses; every standalone number or normalized chart has an adjacent benchmark, comparison, or absolute-magnitude note
rules.prevents: the audience failing to grasp the practical significance or scale of a number, or statistics that feel abstract because a percentage-only view hides practical scale

merged_from.rule: Translate numbers at unfamiliar scale (very large, very small, very fast, very slow) into comparisons with familiar human-scale references.
merged_from.check: scale claims are accompanied by a relatable comparison, not left as a raw unexplained number

rules.rule: Protect a chart's defensibility: display every variable or dimension that could change the audience's conclusion rather than collapsing a multi-dimensional relationship into something that could mislead if an important variable were hidden; position elements in a matrix, segmentation map, or similar chart according to actual measured values, not subjective or impressionistic placement; and don't let a chart's visual sophistication or polish imply more certainty or authority than the underlying data supports.
rules.applies_when: a conclusion depends on more than one variable, a chart positions elements spatially (matrix, segmentation map), or the chart's confidence level is lower than its visual polish suggests
rules.check: ask whether a hidden or omitted variable could support a different conclusion than the one shown; element positions trace back to measured data coordinates, not a judgment call; preliminary or low-confidence findings aren't dressed up in complex, authoritative-looking visualizations
rules.prevents: a technically true but misleading conclusion, a chart that's easily contested because its layout can't be substantiated, and the audience uncritically accepting a conclusion because of misleading visual authority

rules.rule: When a key statistic should be memorable, or when the data describes concrete, recognizable subjects (compounds, sites, products, people), represent it with a relevant icon, pictogram, or photo at the data position rather than a bare numeral or abstract mark — but make sure any icon used is a conventional, unambiguous symbol for what it labels, distinct from decorative chartjunk that carries no data.
rules.applies_when: a statistic is central to the narrative and should stick with the audience, or quantitative data describes identifiable physical subjects
rules.check: the most memorable statistic or concrete-subject data uses an icon/pictogram/photo treatment rather than numeral-only text or an abstract mark; icons used have a conventional, unambiguous meaning
rules.prevents: poor retention of a statistic meant to carry narrative weight, and abstraction disconnecting the audience from what the data actually describes

rules.rule: For long time series (20+ observations) that must fit in a small space, use a sparkline-style miniature rather than averaging the detail away, and always pair it with explicit reference numbers (start, end, min, max, or current value) since the miniature can't carry axis labels.
rules.applies_when: dense, long-running metrics need to be shown compactly, such as operating history or trial enrollment
rules.check: a sparkline encodes 20+ points rather than an aggregated summary; adjacent text states at least the current and reference values
rules.prevents: losing inflections and anomalies to over-aggregation, and leaving a miniature chart with no quantitative anchor

rules.rule: Size time-series charts so the average slope of change reads at roughly 45 degrees — neither so compressed that real swings look flat nor so stretched that noise looks dramatic.
rules.applies_when: setting the aspect ratio (width-to-height) of any trend chart
rules.check: measure the average absolute slope angle in the rendered chart; it falls roughly between 30 and 60 degrees
rules.prevents: a misleading visual impression of how much or how little the underlying data actually changed

rules.rule: On animated data slides, reveal the base chart, equation, or table elements before layering in the assertion highlights (annotations, dashed lines, callouts) that mark the conclusion, and when a complex, multi-layered chart appears in a live, presented deck, build it in sequential animated stages rather than showing it all at once so each stage is independently understandable.
rules.applies_when: a data, equation, or diagram slide uses animation, especially a complex visual in a live presented deck
rules.check: animation order shows underlying data/structure first with conclusion-marking highlights appearing in a later step; complex visuals in presented decks are staged as a build (sent-deck versions can remain static)
rules.prevents: the audience seeing the conclusion before they understand the data it's drawn from, or being overwhelmed by a fully-loaded complex visual before it can be explained

rules.rule: Give labels within the same category of data element identical type size and typeface; when a label carries more than one dimension (category, subcategory, year, location), size and position the broader label above or outside the finer one; and make a chart's or table's reading direction (whether to scan across rows or down columns) unambiguous through labeling, orientation, or spacing rather than leaving the audience to guess.
rules.applies_when: charts or tables with multiple labeled series, multi-dimensional labels, or rows/columns that could be read in more than one direction
rules.check: same-role labels match in size/font; nested labels show a clear size or position hierarchy from broad to specific; a viewer can tell at a glance which direction to read without trial and error
rules.prevents: the audience reading an unintended ranking into a typographic inconsistency, and misread data from an ambiguous reading direction

rules.rule: On line charts over discrete time intervals, mark each measured data point explicitly so the line reads as a connector rather than an interpolation, and keep the spacing between time labels proportional to the actual elapsed time.
rules.applies_when: plotting discrete-interval data (e.g., quarterly or yearly values) as a line chart
rules.check: data points are visibly marked, and equal visual spacing between time labels corresponds to equal actual time intervals
rules.prevents: false implied interpolation between measurements and distorted time comparisons from inconsistent spacing

rules.rule: Remove any visual, textual, or audio element that does not directly support the slide's claim or aid comprehension — decorative template graphics, unexplained frames/borders, mismatched styling, unnecessary complexity — moving anything necessary-but-distracting to speaker notes or the appendix instead of cutting it entirely. Do this before trying to make the key message more prominent, since cutting noise is more effective than adding emphasis.
rules.applies_when: always, when finalizing what appears on a slide
rules.check: For every element, ask whether removing it would reduce understanding of the claim; if not, remove or relocate it. Estimate what share of the slide's area is genuine evidence/claim versus decoration and flag if decoration dominates.
rules.prevents: cognitive overload, diluted focus, and a slide that looks designed but says little
rules.note: Exception: in photographs or other non-quantitative imagery, a thematic or emotional element may stay even if not strictly informative, if it reinforces the message (reynolds-zen).

merged_from.rule: Remove any visual element that exists only for decoration or engagement rather than because it clarifies the claim.
merged_from.check: for each visual element, confirm removing it would make the slide less clear, not just less decorated; flag purely decorative graphics (e.g., stock art, ornamental icons) with no clarifying function

rules.rule: Give the single most important element on a slide the strongest visual weight (size, contrast, color, position), establishing that hierarchy through structural layout first and color/bold as secondary reinforcement; visibly subordinate secondary or contextual elements (smaller, lighter, muted) while keeping them legible; reserve strong emphasis (saturated color, largest size, boldest weight) for at most one or two elements per slide.
rules.applies_when: a slide contains both a primary claim/evidence element and supporting detail
rules.check: Identify what the eye lands on first; confirm it's the intended primary element. Count elements carrying strong emphasis (flag three or more). Confirm secondary elements are smaller/lighter/greyer but still legible.
rules.prevents: minor content competing visually with the slide's actual point, or scattered attention when everything is emphasized at once

rules.rule: Ensure every stylistic variation (size, color, weight, spacing, indentation) maps to a real distinction in importance, category, or relationship; format identical element types identically, similar elements similarly, and different element types visibly differently, so formatting itself communicates structure.
rules.applies_when: styling any recurring element type across a slide or deck
rules.check: For each visual difference, ask what meaning it signals; flag any with no clear answer. Confirm all same-level headings/labels share size and weight.
rules.prevents: the audience misreading unintentional visual differences as meaningful, or missing real distinctions that look the same

rules.rule: When a slide carries a bulleted list, keep it to three to five concise items (never a single bullet; state a lone point as plain text), each no more than two lines, with no sub-bullets beyond one level (CLM-33), introduced by a framing line that says what the list represents. Category-style sets such as agenda entries or chart categories can run to about seven before they should be regrouped.
rules.applies_when: a bulleted or enumerated list appears on a slide, or a set of parallel ideas is being structured
rules.check: Count list items (flag fewer than 3, more than 5, or more than 7 for category lists). Count lines per bullet (flag more than 2). Flag any second nesting level. Confirm a framing line precedes the list.
rules.prevents: lists too long to scan or remember, and dense, hard-to-recall text blocks
curation: Harmonized from 'four to six' to three to five so it agrees with NAR-08 (strong, more authors) and CLM-33 on nesting.

rules.rule: Limit a slide to about four distinct perceptual groupings (text blocks, images, chart panels) that a viewer must attend to separately; merge related ones through visual grouping or split content across additional slides.
rules.applies_when: laying out any slide
rules.check: Count visually distinct groups; if more than four, verify grouping or splitting was considered.
rules.prevents: cognitive overload from exceeding visual working-memory capacity

merged_from.rule: Limit the number of distinct information groups on one slide to four or fewer, with no more than about four sub-items in each group.
merged_from.check: Count the top-level groups and, within each, the sub-items; flag any slide exceeding four and four.

rules.rule: Reveal complex multi-part diagrams, systems, or interrelated elements progressively — one logical group at a time, in narrative order, synced to the narration — rather than showing full complexity at once; never apply this piecemeal reveal to a simple bulleted text list, which should appear whole and not build line-by-line.
rules.applies_when: a slide shows a sequence, process, system, or more elements than can be grasped in one glance, versus a simple text list
rules.check: Does the slide have a defined build order for complex diagrams? Do bulleted text slides appear as a whole, without staged line-by-line reveal?
rules.prevents: the audience being overwhelmed by simultaneous complexity, or a disengaging line-by-line bullet build
rules.note: Resolves the apparent conflict between sources that call bullet-reveal disengaging and sources that call diagram-reveal helpful: the distinction is content type, not a real disagreement.

merged_from.rule: In a live-delivery deck, show a slide's full content at once instead of revealing it line by line.
merged_from.check: confirm slides display complete content immediately rather than disclosing bullets or elements sequentially

curation: Absorbs FAIL-26 (show full content at once). DSN-08 already resolves the split: progressive reveal for complex diagrams and charts, never line-by-line reveal of text lists.

rules.rule: Use a consistent formatting scale (heading size, weight, indentation) so each visual level corresponds to the same logical or abstraction level of the argument throughout the deck, with higher-level ideas staying visually more prominent than the sub-points under them.
rules.applies_when: a deck or slide presents ideas at more than one level of abstraction
rules.check: Every slide or text block at the same logical level uses the same heading size/weight/indentation, and higher-level ideas are visually more prominent.
rules.prevents: formatting that contradicts or obscures the argument's structure

merged_from.rule: Keep visual hierarchy (size, position, emphasis) aligned with the logical hierarchy of the argument.
merged_from.check: confirm nothing is sized, positioned, or emphasized in a way that implies an importance or order different from the actual argument structure

rules.rule: Leave generous whitespace around and between slide elements — roughly 20-30% of the slide area unfilled. If content is dense enough to require sacrificing that whitespace, split it across multiple slides instead of compressing it.
rules.applies_when: always, when laying out any slide
rules.check: Measure the proportion of the slide untouched by content; flag slides with little visible margin, and verify dense content was split rather than crammed in.
rules.prevents: a crowded, overwhelming slide that obscures which elements matter and how they're grouped

rules.rule: Apply one consistent design system across the whole deck — shared grid/alignment, type hierarchy, color palette, image/template style — and keep recurring elements (titles, labels, axis positions, navigation cues) in identical positions on every slide that shares the same structural role.
rules.applies_when: always, across a multi-slide deck
rules.check: Do slide elements align to a shared grid deck-wide? Is each recurring role (title, body, chart-slide layout) styled and positioned identically wherever it recurs?
rules.prevents: a deck that reads as assembled piecemeal, undermining credibility, and forcing the audience to re-locate content on every new slide
rules.note: See tension on consistency vs. deliberate variety for where controlled variation is acceptable.

rules.rule: Use spatial proximity to show which elements belong together, and a visible boundary (border, container, or clear gap) to separate distinct sections or topics on the same slide.
rules.applies_when: a slide contains more than one distinct grouping of information
rules.check: Can a viewer tell at a glance which elements are grouped, and where one section ends and another begins, without reading labels?
rules.prevents: ambiguous grouping that forces the viewer to infer relationships that should be visually obvious

rules.rule: Use animation and slide transitions only when they convey information a static slide cannot — true sequence, process motion, timing, or emphasis tied to narration — never for decoration; avoid content-free transition effects (fades, wipes).
rules.applies_when: considering whether to add animation or transitions to a slide
rules.check: For each animation or transition, name the specific point it clarifies; remove any with no such justification.
rules.prevents: animation that distracts from the message and measurably reduces persuasion and attention versus no effects at all

merged_from.rule: Keep animation sparse, deliberately paced, and synced to narration timing rather than sudden or frequent.
merged_from.check: confirm animation count is minimal, timing lines up with when the speaker would reference it, and no effect triggers abruptly without narrative lead-in

rules.rule: When animation is justified, keep it simple (plain appear/fade) and cap it at roughly four animated or simultaneously-moving stages per slide; avoid decorative motion effects (fly-in, bounce, spin, physics) on the data itself — when animating a chart's own iterations, restrict the effect to appear, disappear, or transparency, and reserve any directional/physics motion for narrative or illustrative elements instead.
rules.applies_when: animation has already been justified as informative for a given slide
rules.check: Count animated stages (flag >4); confirm chart-data animations use only appear/disappear/transparency, with physical motion effects confined to narrative/illustrative elements.
rules.prevents: over-built slides where animation itself becomes a distraction, or motion effects misrepresenting the underlying data

merged_from.rule: Keep entrance fades under about one second and never require the audience to read text while it is still moving or materializing; use one consistent transition style by default, reserving a distinct or novel transition for at most one or two moments of deliberate emphasis in the entire deck.
merged_from.check: Time fade-in effects; confirm text is stationary before it must be read. Count transition styles used (flag more than one default plus two exceptions).

rules.rule: In an animated build, visually de-emphasize (mute color, reduce opacity) secondary or unchanging elements so attention stays on whatever is changing or most important.
rules.applies_when: a slide's animation or diagram has both a key focal element and secondary/context elements
rules.check: The key element retains full color/contrast while secondary elements are visibly muted.
rules.prevents: attention misdirected to non-essential elements, causing the audience to miss the key change

rules.rule: Use color only to encode meaning — emphasis, category distinction, structural signal, recurring theme — never for decoration; once a color is assigned a meaning, keep that mapping identical everywhere it recurs in the deck.
rules.applies_when: applying any color choice on a slide
rules.check: For each non-neutral color, confirm it maps to a specific meaning; trace each color's meaning across slides and flag any reused for a different meaning elsewhere.
rules.prevents: decorative color that adds cognitive load, and the audience having to relearn color meaning on every slide

rules.rule: Verify every color choice in grayscale or a colorblindness simulator and avoid red/green pairings for any meaningful distinction (adjacent chart lines, text/background); keep text/background contrast high.
rules.applies_when: always, when finalizing color choices
rules.check: Convert the slide to grayscale or run a colorblind simulator — is everything still distinguishable? Do any two adjacent elements rely on red vs. green?
rules.prevents: illegibility for viewers with color vision deficiency (roughly 8-10% of men) and for anyone viewing a black-and-white printout

rules.rule: Limit the deck's color palette to roughly one or two accent hues plus neutrals, reserved for elements that need emphasis, reused consistently rather than growing as the deck expands; when brand guidelines mandate specific colors, still cap active accents at one or two and substitute a higher-contrast neutral if a mandated color can't itself serve as a usable accent.
rules.applies_when: selecting or constraining a color scheme for the deck
rules.check: Count distinct non-neutral colors in active use across the deck (flag more than two without a stated reason); confirm brand-mandated colors don't crowd out the emphasis hierarchy.
rules.prevents: a visually chaotic deck where color choices look arbitrary, or color's power as an attention cue getting diluted

rules.rule: Prefer cool or neutral background colors (blue, green) over warm ones (red, orange, yellow), which read as agitating; default to white or light backgrounds for charts and data visualizations specifically, re-selecting colors for contrast only if a dark theme is mandated.
rules.applies_when: choosing a slide or chart background color
rules.check: Is the slide background cool/neutral rather than red/orange/yellow? Are chart backgrounds white/light by default, or, where dark is required, re-tuned for contrast?
rules.prevents: an uncomfortable audience reaction to background color, or data losing visual priority to a heavy background

rules.rule: Use sans-serif typefaces for all on-slide text, and limit the deck to one or two typefaces total, creating hierarchy through size and weight rather than additional font families.
rules.applies_when: selecting typefaces for a deck
rules.check: Is the body/headline typeface sans-serif? Count distinct font families (flag more than two).
rules.prevents: slower reading at presentation distance and off-angle seating, and a busy, inconsistent appearance

rules.rule: Never use underline for emphasis, and avoid setting body text, bullet lists, or data labels in all-caps (mixed case reads faster because word recognition depends on the capital/lowercase silhouette); acronyms are exempt, and all-caps or bold is acceptable specifically for chart titles and legend terms as a scanning aid.
rules.applies_when: formatting any slide text
rules.check: Does any text use underline? Is any non-acronym body/label text set entirely in capitals? Is any all-caps usage confined to chart titles or legend terms?
rules.prevents: reduced legibility from distorted letterforms and slower word recognition

rules.rule: On minimal-text, assertion-evidence-style slides (a headline plus short evidence labels only), set that text in boldface and avoid italics, since bold reads faster at presentation distance; on slides carrying sentence- or paragraph-length text, reserve boldface for navigational elements (headings, labels) and use italics — not bold — to emphasize individual words within sentences.
rules.applies_when: any slide text, split by whether the slide carries sparse evidence labels or full sentences/paragraphs
rules.check: For sparse evidence-label slides: is label text bold with no italics? For sentence/paragraph slides: is bold reserved for headings, with in-sentence emphasis done in italics?
rules.prevents: text too faint to read quickly from the back of a room, or overused bold diluting its value as a navigation cue

rules.rule: Size all text and graphics so they remain legible from the farthest seat in the room at actual presentation scale — for live/projected talks, headline around 28pt, body 18-30pt, citations 12-14pt — and test or simulate this before finalizing.
rules.applies_when: a deck will be presented live or projected
rules.check: Measure point sizes against these ranges; test or simulate legibility from the back of the intended room.
rules.prevents: text or graphics that are technically present but effectively invisible to part of the audience

rules.rule: In read-alone slidedocs, size body columns so lines run about 50-70 characters in left-aligned multi-column layout rather than full-width paragraphs; when the deck will be viewed on a small screen (phone/tablet), increase text size and reduce content density relative to the full-screen version.
rules.applies_when: the deck is meant to be read without narration, or is viewed on a small device
rules.check: Measure characters per line against the 50-70 range; confirm multi-column layout; preview at small-device proportions for legibility and density.
rules.prevents: slow reading and eye strain from mismatched line length, or text becoming illegible on small devices

rules.rule: Follow the audience's natural reading flow (left-to-right, top-to-bottom; positive values to the right and negative to the left on scales): place the title/claim as the largest, top-left element, and place takeaways or recommendations bottom or right rather than top-left.
rules.applies_when: positioning title, summary, and data content on a slide
rules.check: Is the title the largest, top-left element? Are takeaway panels bottom/right? Does the intended eye path match conventional reading order?
rules.prevents: readers starting in the wrong place or reaching the conclusion before the supporting content
rules.note: Eye-tracking data shows Western audiences look upper-left first.

rules.rule: Position a chart's title and axis labels where the audience encounters them before the data (upper-left or top), aligned to their axis in sentence case; place legend/key entries close to and in the same order as the data they label, preferring direct, color-matched labels on the data itself over a separate key whenever space allows.
rules.applies_when: any slide containing a chart or graph
rules.check: Do title/axis labels appear above or left of the data in reading order? Are key entries ordered and positioned to match the display, or replaced by direct color-matched labels where feasible?
rules.prevents: the audience reaching the data before knowing how to read it, or searching back and forth between key and data

rules.rule: Add grid lines to any table larger than 2x2 so viewers can track from row/column headers to specific cells; keep an embedded chart's own caption or title visually subdued (regular weight, neutral color) so it doesn't compete with the data or the slide's main headline.
rules.applies_when: a slide contains a multi-row, multi-column table, or a chart with its own internal caption
rules.check: Confirm grid lines are present in larger tables; confirm chart captions are non-bold and neutral-colored.
rules.prevents: viewers losing their place cross-referencing a table, or a chart caption competing with the data for attention

rules.rule: In dense charts with many closely-spaced elements, reduce line weight and soften line/background contrast to avoid rendering artifacts (moiré, shimmer) that compete with the data; size labels of compared items proportionally to their magnitude so relative scale reads without a legend; set small inline data graphics (sparklines) at text height so they read as part of the sentence rather than a separate figure.
rules.applies_when: a chart has many closely-spaced elements, or lists items of varying magnitude, or uses small inline graphics as evidence within text
rules.check: View the chart at actual display size and check for shimmer/striping; confirm label size tracks magnitude; confirm inline graphics sit at text height.
rules.prevents: chart rendering or labeling that distracts from or obscures the underlying data pattern

rules.rule: Size charts and images proportionally to their content rather than stretching or shrinking them to fill available slide space, and verify any enlarged image retains enough resolution to stay sharp rather than stretching a low-resolution source.
rules.applies_when: placing a chart, graph, or image on a slide
rules.check: Confirm visuals are sized to their content, not artificially stretched; view enlarged images at full display size and check for pixelation.
rules.prevents: distorted or awkwardly scaled visuals, and grainy imagery that reduces credibility

rules.rule: When a single piece of content needs to be especially memorable or attention-grabbing, prefer a large, high-quality photograph over other graphic types, since the eye is drawn to photographs before text or other graphics.
rules.applies_when: choosing how to render a fact intended to be especially memorable
rules.check: For the intended 'sticky' fact, is the chosen visual a large, high-quality photograph?
rules.prevents: a key fact being less noticed or recalled than it would be with a photographic anchor

rules.rule: Crop and size photographic evidence deliberately to emphasize the specific portion relevant to the claim — large enough to read clearly, not so large the slide feels crowded — and orient any directional element within the image (gaze, vehicles, arrows) toward the slide's content or center, never toward the edge or away from the message.
rules.applies_when: a slide includes a photograph, illustration, or icon with an inherent direction
rules.check: Is the image cropped to the relevant portion? Does the implied direction of any directional element lead toward the claim rather than off the slide?
rules.prevents: images included but not actively reinforcing the claim, or unintentionally pulling viewer attention off the slide

rules.rule: Use professional-quality, high-resolution imagery chosen specifically to support the slide's claim and a custom visual template rather than a default software theme; avoid generic stock photography and visual clichés.
rules.applies_when: selecting photographic imagery or establishing a deck's visual template
rules.check: Is each image specific to the content rather than interchangeable stock? Is the template modified rather than an unmodified default?
rules.prevents: loss of credibility and memorability from generic, templated visuals

rules.rule: For diagrams explaining a mechanism, process, or system, use simplified line art rather than a complex or photorealistic image (unless the photorealistic detail is itself the evidence); if adding color or expressive human-like features to increase engagement on such a diagram, apply both together and only to elements essential to the concept, not as general decoration.
rules.applies_when: illustrating a scientific mechanism, process flow, or system relationship
rules.check: Does the diagram show only elements needed to understand the mechanism? If color/human-like features are added, do they appear together and only on essential elements?
rules.prevents: cognitive overload from extraneous visual detail, or a weak or distracting effect from partial or misapplied decoration
rules.note: Distinct use case from the photograph-for-memorability rule: explaining a mechanism vs. anchoring a fact.

rules.rule: Match the visual style and tone of illustrations or photos (realism, polish, seriousness) to the seriousness of the claim they accompany.
rules.applies_when: selecting illustrative imagery for a claim
rules.check: Is the image's style consistent with how seriously the claim should be taken?
rules.prevents: the visual undercutting or contradicting the message's intended tone

rules.rule: Insert a relevant illustrative image at section transitions or after a run of dense, data-heavy slides, and pause briefly when it appears so the audience has time to process it before continuing.
rules.applies_when: transitioning to a new section, or following several information-dense slides in a row
rules.check: Do section transitions or post-dense-content points include a relevant illustration, with speaker notes indicating a pause?
rules.prevents: cognitive fatigue from sustained information density without relief

rules.rule: When a slide contains multiple visual elements meant to be viewed in a specific order, make that order unambiguous — arrange them in natural reading order or add numbered/lettered callouts.
rules.applies_when: a slide has more than one image, panel, or data element requiring a specific viewing sequence
rules.check: Is the intended viewing order obvious without verbal explanation, or are guide marks present?
rules.prevents: audience confusion about which element to look at first and in what order

rules.rule: Place a familiar reference object next to an item whose physical scale matters, so size is conveyed visually rather than relying on a stated number.
rules.applies_when: presenting a physical dimension or scale that a number alone would not make intuitive
rules.check: For any slide asserting a physical size/scale, is a familiar comparison object shown alongside it?
rules.prevents: scale remaining ambiguous despite a verbal or numeric explanation

rules.rule: When overlaying text on a photograph, choose or crop the image so its focal point sits off-center (rule of thirds) or add a contrasting panel, leaving open, legible space for the text, and keep the text the visually dominant layer with the image subdued behind it; vary between symmetric/centered and asymmetric compositions across the deck rather than one pattern throughout.
rules.applies_when: a slide combines a photograph with overlaid text, across a full deck of such slides
rules.check: Is the photo's focal point off-center or contrast-treated where text sits? Does text read easily over the image? Does the deck mix composition patterns rather than repeating one?
rules.prevents: text competing with or obscuring the photo's subject, and static, monotonous slide composition

rules.rule: When a quotation is used as evidence on a slide, set it in large type and visually emphasize the specific phrase that carries the point, rather than presenting the full quote in uniform, undifferentiated text.
rules.applies_when: a slide uses a quotation as primary or supporting evidence
rules.check: Is quote text large enough to read at distance, with the key phrase bolded, colored, or otherwise set apart?
rules.prevents: the audience missing the point of the quote inside a wall of uniformly-styled text

rules.rule: Display DNA, protein, or code sequences in a monospaced font so characters stay aligned; when adapting evidence from a paper or report into a slide, redesign the chart, text, or layout specifically for slide legibility rather than pasting it unchanged from the source.
rules.applies_when: a slide shows a biological/code sequence, or converts evidence from a written source into slide form
rules.check: Is a sequence set in an aligned monospaced typeface? Does the slide's chart/text show signs of restructuring for legibility rather than a direct copy from the source?
rules.prevents: misaligned sequences, and cluttered slides inherited from a document format never designed for projection

rules.rule: Number every slide, and include a slide number or subtle progress/section indicator, whenever a deck will be printed, distributed, shared asynchronously, or has more than about four sections; mark transitions between major sections with a dedicated divider/header slide, and use consistent recurring visual markers (icons, headings) so the audience can always tell where they are in the narrative.
rules.applies_when: the deck will be printed, distributed, shared asynchronously, or has multiple sections
rules.check: Does every slide show a page number or progress marker where required? Does every major section transition have a divider/header slide? Can a viewer identify a slide's place in the structure from visual cues alone?
rules.prevents: confusion when a group discusses specific pages, and the audience losing track of the argument's structure partway through

rules.rule: Limit a live presentation's outline to at most two nested levels (section, sub-point), pushing deeper structure into a written appendix. Within a slide, bullets nest one level at most (CLM-33). Express anything deeper as separate slides or a diagram.
rules.applies_when: structuring a deck's outline, or nesting bullets within a slide
rules.check: Does any section of the live deck require a third structural level? Does any slide nest bullets more than one level?
rules.prevents: a structure too complex for the audience to track without effort during a live talk
curation: The original allowed three to four levels of bullet nesting inside a slide, which contradicted CLM-33 and DSN-05.

rules.rule: In a slidedoc or appendix with three or more hierarchical levels, use numbering that reveals the hierarchy (e.g., 2.4.1) rather than isolated numbers or letters that hide how a section relates to the whole.
rules.applies_when: a slidedoc or appendix has three or more levels of sections/subsections
rules.check: Can a reader infer a section's place in the structure from its number alone?
rules.prevents: readers losing their position within a long document's structure

rules.rule: Give the deck's opening a distinct visual identity (a topic-relevant image on the title slide, and, if using a section map, a distinct recurring icon per section labeled by actual content rather than generic terms like Introduction/Conclusion), and end with a distinct, deliberate closing visual rather than fading text or a bare 'that's all' slide.
rules.applies_when: designing the opening, section-map, and closing slides of a deck
rules.check: Does the title slide include a topic-relevant image? Do section icons recur consistently with specific labels? Does the final slide use a clear graphic signal of closure?
rules.prevents: audience disorientation at the start, losing track of structure partway through, or an anticlimactic ending

rules.rule: Place any logo in a bottom corner rather than the upper-left (reserved for the title), and show it only on the opening and closing slides rather than on every interior slide.
rules.applies_when: a logo appears anywhere in the deck
rules.check: Is the logo in a bottom corner? Does it appear on interior content slides when it shouldn't?
rules.prevents: the logo competing with the title for the audience's first glance, and repetitive visual noise across the deck

rules.rule: Match slide density to delivery mode and audience, and never blend both modes on one slide. In live, narrated, general-audience slides, favor a diagram, image, or single number over prose. Target 30 words or fewer of body text per slide (headline and chart labels excluded) and treat more than about 75 total on-slide words as an overload. Read-alone pages may run denser (SPW-19 sets 100 to 250 words). For technical, expert, or high-stakes audiences, and for appendix or leave-behind material, do not cut evidence just to hit a count. Match density to what full understanding requires.
rules.applies_when: deciding slide density and detail level for a given deck, slide, or audience
rules.check: Live variant: body words per slide 30 or fewer (warn above), total words 75 or fewer (block above). Read variant: governed by SPW-19. Confirm any trim made for brevity is justified by mode and audience, not applied blindly to technical content.
rules.prevents: slides too sparse to stand alone when read, too dense to track when narrated live, or oversimplified to the point of failing an expert audience
rules.note: See tension on the exact on-slide word ceiling for live/general-audience slides, which this rule's ~75-word figure does not fully resolve.
curation: Resolves the DSN on-slide text tension: 30 words is the live body target and 75 words the hard ceiling. The 'six words per slide' figure is dropped because it conflicts with assertion headlines.

rules.rule: Size a read-alone deck to its use case: cap investor/LP pre-reads and prospective-client materials at about 10 pages, and executive-only cover materials at about 5 pages.
rules.applies_when: the deck is meant to be read without narration (pre-read, leave-behind)
rules.check: Count total pages against the stated use case's limit before sending.
rules.prevents: a pre-read too long to fit the reader's available attention window

rules.rule: Design every primary visual (chart, diagram, image) to be understood within a few seconds on its own, without requiring spoken narration to explain it — this matters most for any slide that may be read without a presenter, such as a sent deck or appendix.
rules.applies_when: always for primary evidence visuals; especially critical for sent or read-alone decks
rules.check: Cover the speaker notes/narration; can a first-time viewer state the visual's point from the slide alone within a few seconds?
rules.prevents: a visual that only makes sense with live narration, failing entirely once the deck is sent or read asynchronously

rules.rule: Ensure a slide's visual evidence is already on screen the moment it loads — never show a bare headline over empty space while waiting to reveal the evidence.
rules.applies_when: using an assertion-evidence or evidence-first slide structure
rules.check: On slide entry, is there visible chart/image/diagram content, or just a headline and blank space?
rules.prevents: wasted screen time and a missed opportunity for the audience to process visuals while listening

rules.rule: In a live, in-person presentation in a large venue, blank the screen (or insert a black/white slide) during extended narration with no corresponding visual, or just before the most critical statement, to pull focus from screen to speaker. In a virtual or remote presentation, do the opposite: keep relevant visual content on screen through every transition and pause, since a blank screen reads as dead air rather than deliberate emphasis to remote viewers.
rules.applies_when: a live talk includes a narration segment with no corresponding visual, split by in-person-large-venue versus virtual/remote delivery
rules.check: For in-person large-venue talks, do speaker notes flag where the screen should blank or pause? For virtual/remote decks, does stepping through transitions ever show a blank screen?
rules.prevents: an idle slide competing with the speaker during in-person narration, or remote viewers disengaging during dead screen time
rules.note: Resolves what would otherwise look like a direct conflict (blank the screen vs. never blank the screen) by delivery-mode context: in-person/large-venue versus virtual/remote.

rules.rule: In a webinar, video call, or other remote/self-paced delivery, pace roughly one slide per minute of speaking (or limit each slide's content to what could be explained aloud in about a minute), with each slide's topic tightly matched to what's being said at that moment.
rules.applies_when: webinar, video call, or remote delivery format, or any slide's content density in general
rules.check: Divide expected speaking duration by slide count and confirm it's close to one slide per minute; read the slide's text/visuals aloud and confirm it takes about a minute.
rules.prevents: a static visual sitting on screen long after the narration has moved on, or a slide carrying more than can be explained in the time allotted

rules.rule: When choosing a visual metaphor or concept image to represent an idea, pick one grounded in the audience's own professional domain or documented interests rather than a generic stock concept.
rules.applies_when: using a metaphor or concept-based visual to convey an abstract idea
rules.check: Does the chosen image or metaphor connect explicitly to something documented about this audience's background?
rules.prevents: a metaphor that confuses rather than clarifies because it doesn't land with this specific audience

rules.rule: When a slide includes expandable or linked supplementary content (pop-ups, expandable panels) rather than a separate appendix page, keep it small and positioned so it never covers the primary content it refers to.
rules.applies_when: the deck's appendix or expandable layer is surfaced as an on-slide pop-up or overlay
rules.check: Is any pop-up/overlay panel sized and positioned to leave the referenced primary content visible?
rules.prevents: split attention from having to close or move an overlay to see the content it explains

rules.rule: Keep slide backgrounds plain and visually subordinate — remove decorative stock photography, clip art, patterns, textures, or animated backgrounds that don't present evidence — and never place text over a busy or non-uniform background.
rules.applies_when: always, when choosing slide backgrounds and decorative elements
rules.check: Is the background solid/plain? Is any text sitting on top of a photo, gradient, or pattern rather than a flat area?
rules.prevents: wasted slide space, illegible text, and backgrounds competing with foreground content for attention

rules.rule: Make any intended visual distinction (size, color, contrast difference) large enough to be clearly perceived from the back of the room and at the smallest scale the slide will be viewed; if a difference can't be clearly seen at that scale, remove it rather than leave it as false precision.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: Simulate back-of-room viewing distance and small-scale display; confirm intended distinctions remain clearly perceptible.
rules.prevents: imperceptible differences that convey no real information to the audience

rules.rule: Keep all slide text horizontal; avoid diagonal or rotated text and diagonal connecting lines.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: Scan the draft for any rotated or diagonal text or connector lines.
rules.prevents: reduced readability and a visually messy layout

rules.rule: Invest in visual polish — consistent alignment, deliberate whitespace, typographic care — since audiences judge the credibility of content partly by how polished its presentation looks.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: Confirm alignment, spacing, and typography show deliberate consistency rather than default or careless placement.
rules.prevents: credible content being discounted or disengaged from because it looks sloppily assembled

merged_from.rule: In a live, presented deck, prioritize visual clarity and polish on the opening slides, since audiences form a credibility judgment within the first couple of slides based on visual design and delivery.
merged_from.check: confirm the first two slides are visually clean and strong, and that the deck doesn't rely on later slides to recover from a weak opening impression

rules.rule: Add callouts or emphasis annotations to a chart as separate overlay elements rather than building them into the chart itself, so the visualization and its annotations can be repositioned, reused, or removed independently.
rules.applies_when: highlighting a specific insight within a chart or graph
rules.check: Is annotation text a distinct, repositionable element layered over the visualization rather than embedded in it?
rules.prevents: losing the ability to reposition or reuse the visualization independently of its annotations

tensions.topic: Should individual slide layouts and imagery stay visually consistent across a deck, or deliberately vary to sustain interest?

positions.position: Hold a single consistent design system — grid, alignment, type hierarchy, color palette, template and image style — identical across every slide.
Deliberately vary page layout, eye-path, or image composition (e.g., alternating symmetric/centered and rule-of-thirds asymmetric placement) slide to slide to avoid a monotonous, repetitive feel.

tensions.guidance: Default to the majority position for the deck's structural system: hold grid, alignment, type hierarchy, and color palette fixed deck-wide. Reserve deliberate variation for compositional choices within that fixed system — image placement/cropping, symmetric-vs-thirds framing, chart treatment, or content pacing — never the underlying grid, alignment, or type system itself. Note that reynolds-zen appears on both sides of this split once it's read this way: reuse of colors/fonts/layout is the structural-consistency claim, and rule-of-thirds composition variety is the within-system-variation claim, so the two are compatible rather than contradictory for that source.
tensions.resolution: Kept as resolved in stage 2: fixed grid, type, and palette deck-wide, with variation only in composition inside that system.

tensions.topic: How little text belongs on a live-presented or general-audience slide?

positions.position: Cap total on-slide text at roughly six lines or thirty words, using simple words and round numbers.
Cap on-screen text at six words per slide, pushing everything else into speech.

tensions.guidance: No source-stated context (audience, sent vs. presented) fully resolves this split, and a separate partial rule set attributes a ~30-word figure to reynolds-zen as well, suggesting the six-word figure is this source's aspirational ideal rather than an absolute ceiling. Treat six words as the target for the slide's headline or title text, and thirty words as the hard ceiling for all remaining on-slide text combined (e.g., a short evidence callout). Flag any slide exceeding thirty words as a density violation regardless of style, and flag slides exceeding six words in the headline unless the deck has deliberately committed to a denser, Minto-style text-slide format (in which case the density-by-audience/delivery-mode rule governs instead).
tensions.resolution: The six-word headline guidance is withdrawn because it conflicts with CLM-01 (complete-sentence assertion headlines, 13 sources). Headlines are limited to two lines (CLM-05). Live body text targets 30 words or fewer and blocks above 75 total words (DSN-53). Read pages follow SPW-19.

rules.rule: In live delivery, keep slide body text sparse and non-redundant with speech: short phrases or fragments, graspable in a few seconds, so the audience never has to choose between reading and listening. In read-alone material (slidedoc, pre-read, appendix), write full sentences that stand on their own. Reverse the live default, adding fuller reworded text, when the audience includes non-native speakers, vocabulary is heavily technical, the content needs later search or review, or the deck will also circulate as a reading document. The headline is always a complete-sentence assertion (CLM-01) in both modes.
rules.applies_when: Always. The live branch applies to presented or recorded delivery, the read branch to sent, async, or appendix material.
rules.check: Projected text for a narrated slide is reworded/condensed relative to the speech, not a near-verbatim transcript; roughly under 20 new words per minute of speech, blocks no longer than two lines, main point graspable on a glance; where one of the named exceptions applies, visible text instead carries the fuller explanation in its own reworded form
rules.prevents: split-attention overload from simultaneous reading and listening of the same words; or, in the exception cases, comprehension loss from over-applying the minimal-text default to audiences or content that actually need visible text

merged_from.rule: In a live, presenter-led deck, write slide body text as short phrases or fragments meant to be scanned while the speaker talks; in a slidedoc, leave-behind, or any deck meant to be read without a presenter, write full sentences that stand alone.
merged_from.check: Identify the deck's output mode; for presented decks confirm body text is fragments, not prose; for sent decks confirm claims are complete, self-contained sentences.

curation: Absorbs CLM-21 (fragments live, sentences read). Adds the headline exemption so this rule no longer reads as contradicting CLM-01.

rules.rule: Even on an otherwise sparse, narration-driven slide, render technical terms, equations, specialist vocabulary, and the single most important claim as visible on-screen text spoken aloud at the same time, rather than leaving them to narration alone.
rules.applies_when: a slide introduces a term, formula, or claim the audience must retain or parse precisely
rules.check: Technical terms, equations, and the slide's one key claim appear as short visible labels that are also spoken; everything else that needs lengthy explanation stays in only one channel
rules.prevents: the audience failing to retain or correctly parse a critical term or claim because it was only ever spoken or only ever read
rules.note: Relationship to AUD-04: keep the claim itself in plain language (AUD-04). When a technical term must be spoken, show it on screen as a short label at the same time (this rule). Methodology and justification still go to notes.

rules.rule: Keep a slide limited to its claim plus the one piece of evidence essential to that claim; never make essential evidence available only in speaker notes or an appendix, and never separate an image or chart from the text that explains it (including on appendix pages). Move secondary evidence, methodology detail, and full reference material elsewhere.
rules.applies_when: any slide carrying a claim and supporting evidence, live or in an appendix/handout
rules.check: The evidence the claim depends on is visible on the same slide or page as the claim and its image/chart, not reachable only via notes or a separate appendix section; everything non-essential (detailed methods, secondary data, full tables) sits in notes, appendix, or a linked companion document instead
rules.prevents: audiences who skip or lack access to notes/appendix missing the proof behind a claim, and good evidence going unused because it's disconnected from its explanation

rules.rule: Decide explicitly, before writing individual slides, whether a deck's job is live delivery or standalone reading, and calibrate on-slide text density to that choice throughout: presented decks keep slides to the claim and minimal evidence with everything else in notes; reading decks and slidedocs carry enough context, transitions, and explicit claim-evidence-implication statements that a reader needs no presenter and no prior conversation to follow them.
rules.applies_when: at the start of slide_spec, and whenever a slide or deck will be distributed, emailed, or reviewed independent of live narration
rules.check: The deck is flagged presented or reading/slidedoc and stays consistent with that choice; for reading-mode material, a reader unfamiliar with the talk can state the slide's claim, evidence, and implication from the page alone
rules.prevents: slides too sparse to stand alone when circulated, or too dense and redundant to work as a live visual aid

merged_from.rule: Choose slidedoc-style density — full explanatory text that reads standalone — when the deck will be read without the presenter present (e.g., sent to LPs for async review) or must prep the audience before a meeting; choose presentation-style sparseness, keyed to spoken delivery, when a presenter will be in the room to carry the argument.
merged_from.check: Sent/async decks contain enough standalone text to be understood without narration; live decks are sparse and rely on the presenter for connective explanation.

rules.note: Absorbs SPW-04. When a deck must do both jobs, NAR-31 applies: maintain a live variant and a read variant from one spec.

rules.rule: Structure a reading deck or slidedoc so the full argument can be grasped in roughly 30 seconds by scanning headings and a summary alone, while keeping the body text under each heading self-contained enough to make sense without re-reading the heading.
rules.applies_when: a deck is designed to be read or scanned rather than delivered live
rules.check: A reader following only headings and summary can state the core argument; the body text under any single heading is understandable on its own
rules.prevents: forcing linear reading of material meant to be scanned, and confusion when headings are skimmed without their supporting body text

rules.rule: Before building a full supporting data pack or appendix, test whether a short summary of the claim and recommendation alone lets a reviewer understand and act; add further material only if that test fails.
rules.applies_when: after the storyline is set, before deciding how much supporting material to produce
rules.check: A reviewer can state the recommendation and its basis from the summary alone before any appendix material is built out
rules.prevents: overbuilt presentations whose length obscures the core message

rules.rule: Content that is dense, detailed, or otherwise meant to survive close scrutiny — small-print backup data, full technical records, serious supporting evidence — belongs in a separate handout or appendix document, never on a projected live slide.
rules.applies_when: material requires a density or font size unsuited to projection, or needs to function as a standalone proof document
rules.check: Dense reference-style content is formatted and distributed for reading on paper or device, not projected live; the handout/appendix is intelligible without the presenter
rules.prevents: illegible or overloaded projected slides, and slides forced to double as both a live aid and a full evidentiary record

rules.rule: Build any take-home handout from the presentation's visual elements (diagrams, infographics) repurposed for print, rather than reprinting the slide deck as-is or writing a text-only summary.
rules.applies_when: producing a leave-behind handout to accompany a live presentation
rules.check: The handout contains adapted visuals from the talk, not a plain slide printout or a text-only recap
rules.prevents: a disconnect between the live experience and the take-away reference material

rules.rule: Never put a raw data table on a live-presentation slide; extract and visualize the one insight that matters, and place the full table in the appendix.
rules.applies_when: live presentation containing tabular data
rules.check: No slide shows an unprocessed table during live delivery; a chart or highlighted figure carries the insight instead, with the full table available in the appendix
rules.prevents: the audience reading a table instead of listening to the speaker's point

rules.rule: For categorical data supporting more than one storyline, show a sequence of focused, consistently-ordered, highlighted views when presenting live, but combine those views into one comprehensive chart with text callouts for a version that will be read without a presenter.
rules.applies_when: categorical or multi-series data with more than one defensible narrative
rules.check: The live version shows one consistently-ordered view at a time with highlighting; the circulated/written version shows a single combined chart with callouts
rules.prevents: live audiences overwhelmed by a dense combined chart, or readers of a circulated document missing context a live walkthrough would have provided

rules.rule: When a deck includes backup slides, an appendix, or expandable sections, say so explicitly in the notes or opening remarks, naming what the extra material covers.
rules.applies_when: the deck has backup/appendix/expandable content beyond the main flow
rules.check: Speaker notes or an early slide name the existence of backup material and give a one-line description of its contents
rules.prevents: the audience not knowing supporting material exists, or wasting time on irrelevant optional content

rules.rule: In a remote or teleconference session where the speaker cannot see audience reactions, put the full claim and its supporting evidence directly on the slide rather than depending on verbal delivery alone.
rules.applies_when: remote or teleconference delivery with no visual feedback from the audience
rules.check: Each slide used in a remote session states the assertion and shows the evidence, not just a prompt for the speaker to elaborate
rules.prevents: loss of the message when the speaker cannot gauge comprehension and adjust in real time

rules.rule: When the audience has already received a handout or pre-read before the live session, have the narration synthesize and build on its key points rather than walking through it again page-by-page.
rules.applies_when: a handout or pre-read document was distributed ahead of the live presentation
rules.check: Speaker notes summarize or extend the pre-read's content instead of restating it verbatim in the same order
rules.prevents: wasted live time and audience frustration from hearing material they already read

rules.rule: For technical, scientific, or regulatory claims that will be scrutinized closely, fix the exact required wording — on the slide or explicitly flagged as verbatim in speaker notes — and leave everything else in the notes free for conversational paraphrase.
rules.applies_when: claims involving precise technical, scientific, or regulatory language
rules.check: Technical or regulatory claims appear with exact wording on the slide or are flagged verbatim in notes; other note content is not similarly locked down
rules.prevents: imprecise paraphrasing that invites misunderstanding or loss of credibility among expert reviewers

rules.rule: Put material caveats, risks, and qualifications that affect a claim's validity on the slide itself, not only in speaker notes or an appendix where a reader could miss them.
rules.applies_when: a slide's claim carries a known risk, limitation, or qualification that would change how a decision-maker interprets it
rules.check: Material caveats are visible on the slide, not buried only in notes text
rules.prevents: decision-makers missing a risk or limitation because it was only spoken or filed away in notes

merged_from.rule: When a qualifier, exclusion, or negation is essential to a claim's meaning — leaving it out would flip what the claim says — state it explicitly in the visible claim text, not just in notes. When a qualifier is only needed for full accuracy and doesn't change the claim's core meaning, and it truly won't fit on the slide, move it to notes or appendix rather than dropping it entirely.
merged_from.check: For each qualifier, ask whether omitting it changes the claim's meaning; if yes, confirm it appears in the visible claim rather than only in notes. If no, confirm it's at least preserved somewhere in notes or appendix rather than missing altogether.

merged_from.rule: State the boundary conditions of cited evidence — who it applies to, what outcome it measured, what setting it came from — prominently, not buried in a footnote.
merged_from.check: the boundary condition appears in visible slide text or the first line of notes, not only in a citation or appendix footnote

rules.rule: In live delivery, design the audience-facing slide purely for comprehension. It should not double as the presenter's cue card, and body text should not be written as sentences for the speaker to read aloud verbatim. Assertion headlines (CLM-01) are exempt, as are read-alone decks, where full sentences are required (SPW-01, SPW-19).
rules.applies_when: live presentation only
rules.check: Slide text does not read as a list of speaker reminders; the presenter elaborates on image or data details rather than reading on-screen text
rules.prevents: robotic, read-aloud delivery that damages speaker credibility and audience engagement
rules.note: A minority position (see tensions) holds the slide should also carry the presenter's essential points to avoid broken eye contact; this rule follows the majority view.

merged_from.rule: Never put complete sentences or paragraphs on a slide for the speaker to read aloud verbatim.
merged_from.check: scan slide text for complete sentences or paragraph-length passages; none should exist

curation: Absorbs FAIL-12 ('never put complete sentences on a slide'), rescoped to live body text so it no longer contradicts assertion headlines or slidedoc rules.

rules.rule: When a slidedoc will anchor a meeting, build in dedicated silent reading time — a pre-read window or five to ten minutes at the meeting's start — instead of having the presenter narrate the written content aloud.
rules.applies_when: a slidedoc is the basis for in-person or remote meeting discussion
rules.check: Meeting notes or agenda include an explicit silent-reading window before substantive discussion begins
rules.prevents: participants entering discussion uninformed, or presenters reading written content aloud instead of discussing it

rules.rule: In a slidedoc meant for independent reading, write full sentences rather than fragments, keeping each page to roughly 100 words for concise material and up to about 250 words for denser material.
rules.applies_when: writing slidedoc body copy
rules.check: Word count per page falls in the 100-250 range appropriate to content density; entries are complete sentences, not bullet fragments
rules.prevents: incomplete thoughts that depend on a presenter to fill gaps, or pages so dense they overwhelm the reader

rules.rule: When turning a written document into a live talk, rebuild the content with stories, metaphors, and visuals suited to spoken delivery rather than transcribing the document's text onto slides.
rules.applies_when: adapting an existing written report or memo into a live presentation
rules.check: The presentation includes narrative or visual elements not present in the source document, rather than a slide-by-slide transcription of it
rules.prevents: flat, uninspiring delivery that fails to persuade a live audience

rules.rule: Keep spoken narration temporally and topically locked to whatever is on screen: discuss a visual while it is visible, advance to a new slide only alongside a verbal transition, and reveal dense or multi-part content (one point, bullet, or build step at a time, structure before data) in step with the words describing it, so the audience never reads ahead of or behind the speaker.
rules.applies_when: live presentation with visuals, charts, sequential slides, or multi-step builds
rules.check: Narration content matches the slide currently shown; each reveal/build step corresponds to the narrative point being made at that moment; any element referenced in notes has a matching visible label or pointer
rules.prevents: audience confusion about which element is being discussed, reading ahead and disengaging, or holding narration in memory before the matching visual appears
rules.note: Doumont cautions against pairing any animation with concurrent speech; resolved in favor of Mayer's empirical segmenting evidence — narration synced to a visible, discrete step is supported, while continuous on-screen text should not run concurrently with moving video or animation.

rules.rule: Keep each uninterrupted stretch of narration tied to a single visual to roughly 10-15 seconds (about 25-40 spoken words) before advancing or changing that visual.
rules.applies_when: speaker notes narrate a visual element in a live or recorded presentation
rules.check: Estimated spoken duration of each notes segment tied to one visual stays under ~15 seconds before a visual change
rules.prevents: the transient-information effect, where early narration is forgotten from working memory before a long explanation finishes

rules.rule: Write each slide's speaker notes so the verbal transition to the next idea comes before the slide or visual actually changes, with a brief silent beat during the change; for a data visualization specifically, sequence the notes to orient the audience to the chart, name the axes/legend, identify the pattern, and state the implication, in that order, before transitioning away.
rules.applies_when: writing speaker notes for a slide with a visual that will be advanced or changed live, especially a chart
rules.check: The transition line in the notes appears before any slide-change marker, with a noted pause during the change; chart notes follow the orient-axes/legend-pattern-implication-transition sequence
rules.prevents: audience confusion about whether to read or listen during a slide change, and charts whose notes jump to a conclusion without orienting the audience first

rules.rule: When a slide shows several data points or visual elements at once, speaker notes must say explicitly which element to look at first and why, rather than discussing the slide as an undifferentiated whole.
rules.applies_when: a slide contains multiple charts, data series, or visual elements
rules.check: Speaker notes name the specific element(s) the audience should focus on and state the reason
rules.prevents: audience attention scattering across irrelevant details instead of the evidence that matters

rules.rule: When speaker notes cover a strategic decision or recommendation, include the reasoning that led to it, not only the conclusion.
rules.applies_when: a slide presents a decision, recommendation, or strategic conclusion
rules.check: Speaker notes describe the analysis or comparison that produced the recommendation, not just the final answer
rules.prevents: the audience being unable to evaluate or challenge a recommendation whose reasoning they can't see

rules.rule: When speaker notes include a question or engagement prompt, phrase it as open-ended ('why', 'how', 'what does this tell us') rather than yes/no or multiple-choice, and ask for the audience's reasoning before the supporting evidence is revealed.
rules.applies_when: speaker notes contain an engagement prompt, interactive moment, or self-explanation cue
rules.check: Prompts use open-ended question words with specific guidance on what to address, not generic or closed yes/no phrasing
rules.prevents: passive reception of claims and shallow processing that closed or vague questions produce

rules.rule: Write speaker notes in natural, conversational language — contractions, second-person address, suggestion rather than command phrasing — instead of formal academic or imperative prose.
rules.applies_when: generating speaker notes or narration text for live delivery
rules.check: Notes read naturally aloud, use first/second-person pronouns and contractions, and phrase guidance as suggestions rather than commands
rules.prevents: stiff, distancing delivery that reduces audience engagement

rules.rule: When speaker notes explain why a piece of evidence matters, give the specific magnitude, comparison, or mechanism, not a generic assertion that it is important.
rules.applies_when: speaker notes or slide text assert the significance of a finding
rules.check: Significance statements include a number, comparison, or causal mechanism rather than only 'this matters'
rules.prevents: the audience registering a fact without grasping its significance

rules.rule: Avoid bullet-fragmented lists for complex or analytical reasoning: use connected prose in appendix and handout material, and favor visuals over bulleted text on live-presentation slides, reserving bullets for genuinely sequential steps or spec-like lists.
rules.applies_when: content involves multi-step analytical reasoning in appendix/handout material, or layout decisions for a live-presentation slide
rules.check: Appendix/handout sections presenting an argument use complete sentences showing logical connections rather than bullet fragments; live slides default to a visual or minimal-text treatment unless the content is genuinely a spec or ordered procedure
rules.prevents: loss of the logical connections between ideas, and bullet-heavy live slides that read like documents

rules.rule: Use one consistent term for each concept across slide labels, on-screen text, and speaker notes, and place labels directly on or beside the graphic they identify rather than in a separate legend explained only verbally.
rules.applies_when: always
rules.check: The same term is used for a given concept everywhere it appears; graphic labels are attached to the graphic, not relegated to a key described only in notes
rules.prevents: the audience wondering whether different terms refer to different concepts, or cross-referencing a legend from memory

rules.rule: When a slide shows only an image with no on-screen assertion, make sure the speaker notes contain an explicit spoken statement of the claim that image supports.
rules.applies_when: image-only or visual-only slides with no stated claim
rules.check: Speaker notes for image-only slides contain an explicit sentence stating the claim the image is evidence for
rules.prevents: meandering delivery and audience confusion about what an unlabeled image is meant to show

rules.rule: When a slide must display an excerpt of written source material (a quote, regulatory text, or paper passage), show only the minimum necessary text and have the speaker read it aloud, so text and narration proceed together rather than racing each other.
rules.applies_when: displaying quoted or excerpted written source text on a slide
rules.check: The displayed excerpt is as short as the point requires; the speaker reads it aloud rather than leaving it to be read silently
rules.prevents: the audience reading ahead of or falling behind the speaker while parsing a displayed quotation

rules.rule: Use a blank or black slide during extended Q&A, open discussion, or unscripted storytelling segments that have no visual to show.
rules.applies_when: a live presentation includes a discussion, Q&A, or storytelling segment not tied to a specific visual
rules.check: The slide spec inserts a blank/black slide for these segments rather than leaving a stale or unrelated slide on screen
rules.prevents: a leftover slide competing for attention with the speaker when the visual channel adds nothing

rules.rule: Cut any slide that is not functionally necessary to the spoken narrative — one the presenter's notes never reference and whose removal would not weaken the argument.
rules.applies_when: reviewing a finished or near-finished presented deck
rules.check: For each slide, confirm the speaker notes actually reference it and that removing it would weaken the argument; drop slides that fail this test
rules.prevents: decorative, ornamental slides that pad the deck without supporting the narrative

tensions.topic: Whether the visible slide should also function as the presenter's own cue card

positions.position: The slide should include the essential discussion points visibly, so the presenter can speak from it without breaking eye contact with the audience to check separate notes.
